sens: To circulate continuously from one place to another, like a liquid that flows
To abound, to be rich in (followed by a material complement)
To suffer a loss of substance; to wither (figurative sense)
H2100G.detail:
1. The verb "flow" primarily describes the natural movement of a liquid that runs: water escapes from a spring or flows in a stream. This is the basic meaning of the Hebrew word zuv. In the Bible, it is applied to the water that gushes from the rock struck by Moses (Psalms 78:20: "The Lord made water flow from the rock").
2. The word takes on a figurative and material sense when it qualifies the promised land: "a land flowing with milk and honey." This poetic image means that the land abounds in riches, that milk and honey flow like rivers — that is, they are present everywhere, in inexhaustible profusion. It is the impression of fertility and abundance that the Lord promises to Israel (Exodus 3:8, Deuteronomy 6:3).
3. In ancient Hebrew, zuv can also describe a withering or loss of vigor, like something that flows away and weakens — but this sense is less frequent in the preserved texts.
H2100G.origine: The Hebrew verb zuv comes from a root that evokes continuous movement and flow. It is a simple and vivid root: it paints the natural gesture of a liquid substance that flows and disappears. The same idea is found in other ancient Semitic languages. The word applies literally to water and other liquids, then easily shifts to the figurative (abundance, wealth) or to the physical (loss, weakening).
H2100G.emploi: The verb zuv appears 24 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly to describe the promised land to Israel. The phrase "a land flowing with milk and honey" (eretz zavat halav ud'vash) is a refrain of the Pentateuch and the Prophets: Exodus 3:8, 3:17, 13:5; Numbers 13:27, 14:8; Deuteronomy 6:3, 11:9, 26:9, 26:15, 27:3, 31:20; Joshua 5:6; Jeremiah 11:5, 32:22; Ezekiel 20:6, 20:15. This phrase becomes emblematic of the divine promise and the abundance that Israel expects. It is also found for miraculous water (Psalms 78:20, 105:41; Isaiah 48:21) and for material blessings (Jeremiah 49:4).
H2100G.portee: This word reveals how God speaks to His people in concrete and desirable images. The image of milk and honey flowing paints not just a simple promise of territory, but a life of abundance and rest. For the Christian reader, it reminds us that God promises not just the bare necessities, but generosity and richness — and that His promises are expressed in terms we can imagine and desire.

sens: Physical outflow of the body, disease or pathological state
Liquid or fluid emission from the body
State of ritual impurity related to this outflow
In a figurative sense: moral decay or ruin
H2100H.detail:
1. The word first designates an abnormal outflow from the human body: a disease that causes a secretion or continuous oozing. In Leviticus 15:2, it refers to a disease in a man (gonorrhea), and in Leviticus 15:19 and 15:25, to a flow of blood in a woman beyond her normal periods — a kind of chronic hemorrhage.
2. The word describes the continuous and abundant nature of this outflow: it is not an isolated drop, but an emission that persists and soils everything the person touches or sits on (Leviticus 15:9: the mount becomes impure).
3. In the law of Moses, having a flow renders the person ritually impure for a determined period. This impurity is transmitted by contact: anyone who touches the sick person or their clothing is unclean until evening (Leviticus 15:7). Purification only occurs after healing and a specific ritual (Leviticus 15:13).
4. Used figuratively in 2 Samuel 3:29, the flow expresses a ruin or continuous decay: it is a curse that slowly consumes the one it strikes, like a disease that exhausts them.
H2100H.origine: The Hebrew verb zuv literally means "to flow" or "to run out." It evokes the image of a liquid that flows continuously, that spills out of its limits. It is a concrete word, derived from the observation of natural phenomena: water flowing, blood running. In the Old Testament, this word specifically applies to impure bodily discharges according to the Mosaic law.
H2100H.emploi: This verb appears 16 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in chapter 15 of Leviticus, which entirely deals with the impurity due to bodily discharges. It is a law of ritual purity that distinguishes normal discharges (regular menstruation) from abnormal discharges (prolonged or excessive flows). The word is also used to describe the effect of contact: what is touched by the afflicted person becomes impure. In 2 Samuel 3:29, it appears in a curse from King David against the house of Joab, where it takes on a figurative sense of decay or moral ruin. The context always shows a notion of defilement, ritual contagion, and the necessity of purification.
H2100H.portee: For the Christian reader, this law of Leviticus reveals the holiness of God and the attention He pays to the purity of the people of Israel. These rules also teach that everything affecting the human body — disease, suffering, mortality — places the one experiencing it at a distance from divine holiness, but that purification and forgiveness are always possible. Jesus, in healing the woman with a flow of blood (Mark 5:25-34), shows that grace surpasses the laws of ritual purity and that faith restores authentic communion with God.

sens: To weaken progressively until death
To flow, to run out (in a physical sense)
To wither from hunger or disease
H2100I.detail: 1. The primary sense is the image of a liquid that flows and exhausts: a spring that runs dry, a life that slips away drop by drop. This is why the word also designates both physical outflow (a hemorrhage, a bleeding wound) and the decline of a person who dies slowly. 2. Applied to a person, the verb depicts someone who is withering: it speaks of fading, consuming, losing strength day by day. In Lamentations 4:9, the besieged of Jerusalem die "exhausted," drained of their substance by hunger — a slow and painful death, worse than that of the sword. 3. The word also evokes blood flow or bodily discharges: in the Law, these flows render impure the one who is afflicted, because they signify a loss of vitality.
H2100I.origine: The Hebrew verb zuv comes from a root that paints the movement of a liquid that flows and disappears — hence the image of flowing, drying up, melting. Nowhere in the Old Testament does this verb form a rich verbal family; it remains isolated, but its image is very concrete: water that goes away is the strength that goes away.
H2100I.emploi: The word appears only once in the Segond in Lamentations 4:9, in the context of the siege of Jerusalem by the Babylonians in 586 B.C. It describes the inhabitants of the city ravaged by hunger, exhausted, who perish slowly and miserably. The usage highlights the cruel contrast: those who fall by the sword die quickly and without prolonged suffering, while those who die of hunger exhaust themselves, slowly consuming away, body and soul. It is the very image of agony.
H2100I.portee: This word reminds the reader that slow death, gradual exhaustion without hope, is one of the most terrible forms of God's judgment. It also teaches us that God sees all suffering, even that which drags on without witness: the exhausted of Jerusalem are not forgotten. For the believer, it is an invitation to place trust in God when weakness assails us, for He alone can revive us.

sens: involuntary discharge of a substance from the human body
abnormal loss of semen in men
abnormal or prolonged bleeding in women
state of ritual impurity caused by this discharge
H2101.detail:
1. The word refers to a pathological discharge from the body — not a natural secretion, but an involuntary and abnormal loss. In Leviticus 15:3, a man suffering from gonorrhea remains unclean "whether his flesh discharges his flow or whether it holds it back": it is the discharge itself, or the disease causing it, that renders him unclean.
2. In men, it refers to a loss of semen due to a venereal disease (gonorrhea). The Law treats this condition as resulting in ritual impurity that persists even after healing: in Leviticus 15:13, the one who is purified from his flow must wait seven days and make an offering.
3. In women, the flow can be an abnormal menstrual bleeding — either outside of regular periods or of excessive duration. Leviticus 15:25 speaks of a woman "whose flow lasts longer than usual": as long as this abnormal discharge lasts, she remains unclean.
4. In all cases, the flow places the one suffering from it in a state of legal impurity. This impurity is not a moral condemnation, but a ritual separation: it prevents access to the sanctuary and affects those around (whoever touches a woman with a flow becomes unclean until evening).
H2101.origine: The Hebrew word זוֹב comes from a root meaning "to flow, to run." It is an abstract noun derived from the verb: it denotes the action or state of that which flows. The same root is used to describe other liquid discharges or natural flows. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), this Hebrew word is translated by Greek terms that emphasize the pathological discharge and ritual impurity.
H2101.emploi: The word appears ten times in the Bible, exclusively in Leviticus 15 (the section on bodily impurities). It designates two categories of discharges: in men, a venereal disease (gonorrhea); in women, abnormal or prolonged bleeding. The Law treats these two cases under the same regime of impurity, but with different details: for men, the flow causes an impurity that persists until purification and offering (Leviticus 15:13-15); for women, the impurity lasts for the duration of the flow, and it also affects those who touch her (Leviticus 15:19, 25). The flow is never moralized: the Law acknowledges a physical reality and draws ritual consequences from it.
H2101.portee: This passage reveals how the Levitical Law sought to maintain the ritual purity of the community and the sanctuary in light of the realities of the human body. For today's believer, this shows that the Old Testament does not deny illness or bodily weaknesses: it recognizes them and seeks to integrate them into the liturgical order. Jesus, by healing the woman with a hemorrhage (Mark 5:25-34), fulfills the law by restoring the purity and dignity of those whom illness rendered ritually excluded.

sens: to boil, to cook at high heat
to show arrogance, to behave with haughtiness
to defy someone with impudence
to act wickedly, malice
H2102.detail:
1. The primary and concrete meaning is "to boil" or "to cook": the stew that Jacob prepares "boils" at high heat (Genesis 25:29). It is an image of heat and intense agitation.
2. From this boiling arises a moral image: that of arrogance and pride that "boil" within someone. The person who "acts with pride" behaves in a haughty manner, refuses obedience, and believes themselves above the law (Deuteronomy 17:13). They surrender to their arrogance as if it were a feeling that consumes them.
3. The word also describes the insolence that leads one to defy someone, to challenge an order: to show "audacity" by going up the mountain against the Lord's command (Deuteronomy 1:43), or by having the audacity to speak in His name without being authorized (Deuteronomy 18:20).
4. It can finally denote the malice that manifests: to act "wickedly" or with "wickedness" towards one's neighbor (Exodus 21:14). It is the concretization of this pride into harmful acts.
H2102.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that first evokes the action of boiling, agitating. The family also includes a derived noun (zédon, זְדוֹן) meaning "presumption, arrogance." This transition from the concrete to the figurative is typical of Hebrew: the boiling of water becomes the symbol of the arrogance that troubles the heart and conduct. In Aramaic, the same word exists with the meaning of "to be proud."
H2102.emploi: The verb appears about ten times in the Old Testament. In Genesis 25:29, it retains its very concrete meaning of cooking. Elsewhere, in the laws of Exodus and Deuteronomy, the meaning shifts towards moral arrogance and disobedience: the one who violates the law does so "with audacity" (Deuteronomy 18:20), the one who acts wickedly "acts" thus voluntarily (Exodus 21:14). The verb particularly describes the rebellions of the Israelites: they "show themselves rebellious" to the Lord (Deuteronomy 1:43; Nehemiah 9:16, 9:29), they "surrender" to pride despite warnings. It is a voluntary sin, a conscious and deliberate rebellion.
H2102.portee: This word reminds the believer that pride is not a passive flaw: it is an action, a "rebellion" against God that manifests in our choices and words. Scripture never presents arrogance as an excusable weakness, but as an act of voluntary disobedience. Recognizing this word invites each person to examine whether they are not "acting with pride" in their own life — refusing counsel, defying a restraint that God places upon them, or speaking without His authorization.

sens: To act with pride and presumption
To behave in a haughty and contemptuous manner towards others
To refuse to acknowledge one's limits or the authority of others
H2103.detail:
1. To act with pride and presumption: it is to behave insolently, believing oneself superior or invulnerable. In Daniel 5:20, King Nebuchadnezzar is cast down from his throne precisely because "his spirit was hardened to arrogance" — he allowed himself to be inflated with pride and forgot who he really was.
2. To behave in a haughty manner: it is to despise others, refusing to listen to or respect them. Arrogance isolates the one afflicted by it and blinds them to reality.
3. To refuse to recognize one's limits: it is to deny one's dependence on God or any higher authority, believing oneself above the rules. This is exactly the sin of King Nebuchadnezzar, who had to learn at his own expense that no earthly power escapes divine judgment.
H2103.origine: The Hebrew verb zud expresses the idea of rising up, standing tall, acting with misplaced pride. It describes an attitude of the heart that swells and hardens. This word belongs to the biblical vocabulary of spiritual pride, which must be distinguished from healthy assurance: it always speaks of a presumption that goes against God or wisdom.
H2103.emploi: This verb is infrequent in the Hebrew Bible. Its sole use in Daniel 5:20 places it in a context of divine judgment on a powerful king. Nebuchadnezzar embodies the very type of prince who, dazzled by his power, forgets that all power comes from God and that pride precedes a fall. This account teaches that arrogance does not escape God's gaze, even among the greatest kings.
H2103.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that pride is a constant temptation of the human heart, especially for those who have power or success. God resists the proud and humbles the lofty. He invites everyone to vigilance: cultivating humility, recognizing one's limits and dependence on God, is to place oneself under blessing rather than judgment.

sens: Ancient people mentioned only once in the Bible
Presumed inhabitants of the eastern region of Ammon, beyond the Jordan
H2104.detail:
1. The Zuzim are an ancient people about whom we know very little, as the Bible mentions them only once, in Genesis 14:5. They appear in the account of the wars waged by Kedorlaomer and his allies against the peoples of Canaan and neighboring regions.

2. According to the etymology of the Hebrew name, the Zuzim could be "wandering creatures" or nomads. They likely inhabited the ancient region of Ammon, east of the Jordan — an area we know better through other biblical peoples like the Ammonites, who became its main inhabitants.
H2104.origine: The Hebrew name זוּזִים (Zuzim) derives from the verb שׁוּז (shouz), which evokes the idea of moving about, wandering, or being busy here and there. This name suggests a people of nomadic or semi-nomadic shepherds. The etymology explains why these "wandering" creatures were found in the steppe and semi-desert regions east of the Jordan, ideal areas for grazing and pastoralism.
H2104.emploi: The Zuzim are mentioned only once in the Bible, in Genesis 14:5. In this passage, they are mentioned alongside other ancient peoples — the Rephaim, the Emim — all of whom were defeated by Kedorlaomer and his kings during a military campaign in Abraham's time. This isolated mention shows that they formed a sufficiently distinct and powerful people to be noted in historical accounts, but they had probably disappeared or been assimilated before the later biblical traditions were written down.
H2104.portee: The mention of the Zuzim reminds us that the ancient Near East was home to many peoples now forgotten. Their brief appearance underscores the historical reality of the world that Abraham traversed, populated by diverse nations. This detail lends a certain authenticity to the account in Genesis 14, which accurately lists the political and military actors of that distant time.

sens: A man from the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible
H2105.detail: Zocheth is a character from the Old Testament belonging to the tribe of Judah, living during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. He is the son of Ishi and the brother of Ben-Zocheth. His name appears only once in the biblical genealogies, in 1 Chronicles 4:20, where he is listed among the descendants of Judah.
H2105.origine: The name Zocheth means "the one who releases" or "the one who lets go." It derives from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of letting go or setting free. Few details are known about the exact etymology, but the name reflects a reality or quality of the character it designated.
H2105.emploi: Zocheth is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:20, in a genealogical list of the descendants of Judah. He is presented as the son of Ishi, alongside his brother Ben-Zocheth. These genealogies in the book of Chronicles preserve the memory of the families of Judah and their branches during the period of the divided monarchy. Zocheth plays no particular role in biblical history; he represents a simple link in the genealogical chain of Israel.

sens: Angle of a construction, where two surfaces meet
Protruding part of an object or structure
Hidden or secluded place
H2106.detail:
1. The corner is the angle formed where two surfaces of a building or object meet. In Zechariah 9:15, the expression "the corners of the altar" refers to the four protruding angles of the sacrificial altar, prominent and striking parts of this sacred object.
2. By extension, it is a protruding part that stands out. In Psalms 144:12, our daughters are compared to "carved columns that adorn the palaces" — the Hebrew word translated here as "columns" (زاوِية) evokes rather the architectural elements in relief, the worked angles that beautify royal edifices.
3. The corner can also refer to a separate place, a defined space, often a refuge or a particular location within a construction.
H2106.origine: The word זָוִית (zavit) comes from a root that expresses the idea of turning, changing direction. The angle is precisely the place where a direction changes, where two lines or surfaces meet at a certain angle. The same family of words also expresses the idea of "diverting" or "bypassing" — hence the image of the corner as a place that makes a detour from the straight line.
H2106.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Psalms 144:12, it refers to ornamental architectural elements — the columns or protruding angles — that beautify royal palaces, in an image of beautiful and well-formed young women. In Zechariah 9:15, it refers to the corners of the altar, those protruding angles where the blood of sacrifices was poured and which had ritual significance in Israelite worship. In both cases, the word evokes something notable, visible, that is part of a structure.
H2106.portee: This word reminds us that the beauty of a human being, whether man or woman, lies in a complete harmony where each element has its place — like the well-proportioned angles of a well-built structure. By speaking of the corners of the altar, the Bible emphasizes that even the architectural details of worship contribute to the glory of God and are imbued with sacred significance.

sens: To pour out, to abundantly spill a liquid or material
To treat with disdain, to scorn
To waste, to squander without measure
H2107.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to pour literally: in Isaiah 46:6, the idolaters "pour" the gold from their purse, meaning they spill it, spend it abundantly to finance the making of an idol. It is the image of a flow, of abundance poured out without restraint.
2. The word can also express disdain or contempt: in Lamentations 1:8, those who once honored Jerusalem now "despise" her upon seeing her nakedness and shame. It is to treat someone or something without regard, to belittle.
3. Between these two meanings, the idea of waste or prodigality emerges: to pour something is to dispose of it without counting, to spend it or to cast it away. The word encompasses both the act of pouring and the indifference with which it is done.
H2107.origine: The Hebrew root zul evokes the movement of what flows, spreads. It is rare in biblical Hebrew, with only two documented uses. The fundamental idea is one of a violent or abundant action: one pours, spreads, disperses. The transition from one meaning to another (from the concrete act of pouring to the abstract sense of disdain) can be understood through gesture: to despise is also to "push away," similar to the gesture of pouring away from oneself.
H2107.emploi: The verb zul appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Isaiah 46:6, in the active form, it describes the act of pouring out gold: the idolaters "pour" precious metals without counting to shape their gods, revealing the absurdity of idolatry. In Lamentations 1:8, in a form expressing rather disdain, it shows how once-honored Jerusalem becomes an object of contempt. These two uses, though rare, illustrate how a simple verb of physical movement can shift to an emotional or moral sense.
H2107.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on two forms of folly: that of squandering one's goods for worthless idols, and that of reducing to nothing a glory or dignity once recognized. The fall of Jerusalem in Lamentations shows how contempt arises from the abandonment of God. For the Christian, pouring gold to idols becomes an image of what is given to the false gods of our time; and contempt for the fallen reminds us of the biblical call to mercy rather than judgment.

sens: What remains when one or more things are removed
A restriction: something is excluded from the rest
With the exception of, excluding, except for
H2108.detail:
1. The word comes from a root that means "to remove, to set aside." It literally refers to what remains after something has been put aside: imagine a group where one person is removed, and what remains is "except that person." In Deuteronomy 1:36, all the adult Israelites will die in the desert, "except" Caleb — he alone will be spared and possess the land.

2. The word functions as a logical restriction: it delineates what is excluded from a general statement. In Joshua 11:13, Israel does not burn any city "except" Hazor; in 2 Samuel 7:22, "there is none like you, and there is no other God but you" — David excludes all other gods. It is a way of saying: "In this broad statement, remove this, and you will have the truth."

3. The word is used to indicate one or more exceptions to a rule. It creates a clear separation between what applies and what is exempt. In Psalms 18:32, "who is God except the Lord?" — one seeks an equivalent, there is none, the Lord alone remains unparalleled.
H2108.origine: The Hebrew root means "to remove, to set aside." It evokes the concrete gesture of separation: one takes and sets aside. The word thus designates what remains once the subtraction is made. In Aramaic, a related root has the same meaning. This vocabulary is found in formulas of exclusion or reservation throughout Scripture.
H2108.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in poetry and in the narratives of the Old Testament. It is used as a preposition or conjunction to exclude. In Deuteronomy 1:36 and 4:12, it marks exceptions to God's judgments; in Joshua 11:13 and Ruth 4:4, it specifies a practical restriction. The prophets Isaiah use it to affirm the uniqueness of God (Isaiah 45:5, 45:21): "I am the Lord, and there is no other" — no other god exists. The Psalms use it to exalt God: in Psalms 18:32, it is a rhetorical question where the exception confirms divine singularity.
H2108.portee: This word encapsulates a central biblical truth: the uniqueness and incomparability of God. Each time it excludes everything that is not God, it teaches the reader that no creature, no power can equal the Lord. For the believer, recognizing these exceptions — "no one is like you" — affirms their trust: only God is reliable. It is also learning to discern: the Word of God sets limits, exclusions that protect and guide us.

sens: To provide someone or an animal with sufficient and regular food
To be in good physical health, thriving due to abundant nourishment
Figuratively: overflowing with vital force and energy, to the point of becoming uncontrollable or unrestrained
H2109A.detail:
1. The verb primarily means to feed, to provide the necessary food for someone or an animal to live and grow.
2. One who is well-nourished is in good physical condition: plump, vigorous, healthy, like a well-fed animal that has strength.
3. In the imagery of Jeremiah 5:8, well-fed horses become untamed and impulsive: they have so much energy that they expend it uncontrollably, running "here and there," neighing after other men's wives. Excess physical well-being produces moral excess there.
H2109A.origine: The Hebrew verb zun likely comes from an ancient root meaning "to feed" or "to sustain." It belongs to the family of words related to nourishment and maintenance. The form used here (hophal, the passive form) emphasizes the resulting state: being fed, having been well treated.
H2109A.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 5:8. The prophet uses it in a vision of the well-fed horses of Judah to criticize the luxury and debauchery of the wealthy of his people: stuffed with well-being, they lose all moral restraint and chase after other men's wives. The image transposes to the sexual sphere the idea that unrestrained physical well-being leads to transgression.
H2109A.portee: This word reminds us that material abundance is not bad in itself, but it requires wisdom and self-control. A comfortable life can become dangerous when not accompanied by the fear of God and respect for others. It is a warning against the danger of prosperity without justice.

sens: Food, what one eats to live
What nourishes, sustains
Figuratively: what maintains or strengthens something immaterial
H2110.detail:
1. The word primarily designates concrete food, what is consumed for nourishment. In Daniel 4:12, the giant tree abundantly bears "food" intended for all the animals that come to feed on it: it is the substance that sustains life.
2. More broadly, it means everything that nourishes, sustains a living being — not only physical food but general sustenance.
3. Figuratively, food can also maintain or strengthen what is immaterial: a word, a thought, a virtue. The word evokes what "gives life" in the fullest sense.
H2110.origine: The Hebrew root zun belongs to the Semitic family of verbs of "sustenance." The verb fundamentally means "to nourish" or "to sustain" (to provide food, to supply for sustenance). The itpéal form (or reflexive passive) "zu na" means "to feed oneself" or "to be fed." The word is related to the idea of regularly providing for vital needs.
H2110.emploi: The word appears only once in biblical Hebrew, in the vision of the tree of kingdoms in Daniel 4:12. There it designates the abundant production of the mythical tree that becomes a source of sustenance for all living beings on earth. This unique usage shows how the kingdom-tree fulfills its vital function: it does not keep its fruits for itself, but shares them with all that exists. The image is one of creative generosity, an inexhaustible resource put at the service of life.
H2110.portee: This word reminds us of the responsibility of the one who reigns, of the one who "bears fruit": not for themselves alone, but to nourish all those who depend on it. For the Christian reader, it also evokes how Christ himself gives himself as food ("I am the bread of life"), and how each believer, bearing spiritual fruit, must share it to sustain others.

sens: To move back and forth or up and down quickly and involuntarily
To be shaken by fear or dread
To show respect or submission through body language
H2111.detail:
1. The verb first describes a physical movement of vibration or agitation: the whole body or a part of the body trembles, shakes, like an object that quivers. It is an involuntary trembling, a rapid oscillation. In Ecclesiastes 12:5, "the keepers of the house tremble" depicts the effects of old age: hands and limbs lose their stability and move uncontrollably.
2. The word then evokes terror, the dread that seizes someone: the trembling becomes the visible sign of intense fear or violent emotion. It can also convey a fearful reverence, like the respect due to a formidable authority.
3. In Esther 5:9, "to move" before someone means to show deference through gesture: Mordecai refuses to rise or move before Haman, thus rejecting the homage that is demanded of him. It is a matter of honor and submission.
H2111.origine: The Hebrew verb זוּעַ (zua) belongs to a family of images related to sudden and involuntary movement. The root suggests agitation, a jolt. In Aramaic, the equivalent word exists with the same meaning: "to tremble, to be agitated." The image starts from the physical body that quivers, but it quickly extends to the soul: one who trembles in fear, one who shakes in dread.
H2111.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Esther 5:9, it describes Mordecai's refusal to pay homage to Haman through gesture (זוּעַ in the sense of "to move, to shake"). In Ecclesiastes 12:5, it paints old age: "the keepers of the house tremble," a poetic image of the trembling hands of one who is aging (intensive Pilpel: "tremble greatly"). A third occurrence in Habakkuk 2:7 completes the picture: trembling as a reaction of fear. The word thus evokes both the absence of voluntary movement of deference and the involuntary movement of the body seized by fright.
H2111.portee: This word helps us understand how Scripture views fear and reverence: they manifest concretely, through the body that shakes or becomes still. It is a reminder that faith is not just a matter of the mind, but engages the whole person. Old age and human frailty also find their expression in this image of trembling: the Psalms and Ecclesiastes show the mortal condition of man as a physical reality that God sees.

sens: To be afraid, to be seized with fear in the presence of something or someone impressive
To be agitated by shivers or involuntary movements
H2112.detail:
1. The verb denotes the shiver of fear that seizes someone in the face of a formidable power. In Daniel 5:19, all the peoples trembled before King Nebuchadnezzar because of his greatness and absolute authority: this trembling expresses both physical fear and the fearful respect inspired by an overwhelming power.
2. More broadly, to tremble is to be agitated by involuntary movements — whether it is fear that makes the body sway, or the awareness of being faced with a reality that surpasses man and shakes him.
H2112.origine: The Aramaic word zu.a (זוּעַ) comes from a root that expresses agitation and shivering. It is the Aramaic equivalent of the cognate Hebrew verb (זוּעַ, H2111), both evoking the involuntary movement of the body. The Hebrew root literally depicts the jolt, the physical trembling.
H2112.emploi: The verb appears twice in the Bible, exclusively in the book of Daniel (5:19 and 6:26), which is not surprising since Daniel is written in Aramaic from 2:4. In both cases, it describes the reaction of fear that a supreme authority inspires: first, the fear that the peoples feel before King Nebuchadnezzar, then that which the peoples feel in response to King Darius's decree regarding the living God. The context is always one of absolute domination inspiring terror.
H2112.portee: This verb reminds us that fear is a natural and bodily reaction before something greater than oneself. For the Christian reader, it raises the question: before what power do we tremble? Before the great ones of this world, or before the God who holds all true authority?

sens: Intense fear, sudden terror that seizes
A spectacle of horror that inspires terror
Trembling or shivering caused by fear
H2113.detail:
1. The word first denotes a violent and sudden fear, a fright that paralyzes: in Isaiah 28:19, the prophet announces that divine judgment will pass every day and every night, and the mere sound of this judgment "will cause terror," meaning it will seize people with dread.
2. The "terrifying" is also the very thing that provokes this fear — the object of terror. It is what causes horror, what chills to the bone.
3. The word also evokes physical shivering, the trembling of the body seized by fear — as if terror manifests itself in the body.
H2113.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root (זוע) that means "to tremble" or "to agitate." This root itself paints the image of convulsive movement, of agitation from fear. The word זְוָעָה is a derivative: it is the trembling that comes from fear, or the fear that causes trembling. The fundamental notion is the involuntary movement of the body seized by terror.
H2113.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 28:19. The prophet speaks of God's judgment that will fall upon Judah: this judgment will pass like a crashing wave, every morning, every day and every night, and its mere sound will cause a "terror" to those who endure it. The context suggests a repeated, oppressive, almost inevitable terror — it is the fear of one who sees punishment coming without being able to prevent it.
H2113.portee: This word reminds us that the judgment of God inspires a legitimate fear. For the believer, it invites us to take seriously the gravity of sin and the reality of divine judgment. But it also calls for repentance: one who trembles before God can still turn to His forgiveness.

sens: one who does not belong to a group, family, or nation
one who does not have the right to access a place or function reserved
the foreign woman, particularly a woman who seduces outside of marriage
one who is hostile or an enemy
one who has turned away from God or His ways
H2114A.detail:
1. A stranger is someone who comes from elsewhere, who does not belong to the people, family, or group in question. In the laws of Leviticus and Numbers, it refers to one who is not consecrated or does not have the required status: "No stranger shall approach you" (Numbers 18:4) means that one cannot allow just anyone to approach worship or the sanctuary.
2. The stranger is also one to whom certain places or actions are forbidden. Only the priests could eat certain sacrifices: "No stranger shall eat of it, for they are holy things" (Exodus 29:33). This is a barrier of separation based on status or consecration.
3. In Proverbs, the "foreign woman" refers to a woman who is not a wife, particularly one who seduces with her sweet words and leads to infidelity or immorality (Proverbs 7:5). It is an image used to speak of temptation.
4. The stranger can be one who opposes us or is hostile: "Strangers have risen against me, violent men seek my life" (Psalms 54:5). The word then takes on a nuance of enemy or aggressor.
5. Figuratively, being a stranger to God means turning away from Him: "Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers" (Lamentations 5:2) expresses loss and alienation when one no longer truly belongs to God.
H2114A.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of becoming other, separating, or turning away. The word can function as an adjective (something or someone that is strange, out of the ordinary) or as a participle (one who is a stranger, who does not belong to the group). In biblical Hebrew, it describes both physical strangeness — one who comes from another place — and social or moral strangeness — one who is separated, excluded, or has become an enemy.
H2114A.emploi: This word appears 75 times in the Old Testament, mainly in legal texts (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers), Psalms, Proverbs, and the prophets. In cultic laws, it is an essential notion: the stranger, the non-consecrated, cannot participate in sacred rites, eat offerings, or approach the sanctuary — this underscores the holiness of God which demands a clear separation between the sacred and the profane. In Proverbs, the term mainly applies to the "foreign woman" who represents the temptation of infidelity and sin. In Psalms and the prophets, it takes on a hostile dimension: the stranger becomes the enemy, one who threatens or oppresses the people. The meaning thus varies from simple legal status to total hostility.
H2114A.portee: Understanding this notion of stranger illuminates how God organizes His people around holiness and separation from what defiles. For the Christian reader, it shows that access to God is not automatic: it requires consecration and a condition. It is also a warning against the allure of "foreign women" — that is, against anything that seduces outside the path that God proposes. Finally, the word reminds us that becoming a stranger to God means putting oneself apart from His blessing.

sens: That which provokes disgust, repulsion
That which incites aversion or rejection
H2114B.detail:
1. This word expresses what is unpleasant, repulsive, provoking physical or moral aversion. In Job 19:17, Job says that his mood has become a "burden" to his wife — meaning that his breath or behavior has become repugnant, to the point that she rejects him.
2. Figuratively, it denotes what provokes moral or social rejection: one who is afflicted by illness or defilement becomes repugnant in the eyes of others, which accentuates their isolation and suffering.
H2114B.origine: The Hebrew verb zur belongs to a family of words expressing disgust and aversion. The root evokes a visceral reaction, an instinctive rejection of something impure or offensive. The participle, used here, describes a permanent state or quality: one who provokes disgust.
H2114B.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in the context of Job's extreme suffering. Stricken by illness, Job observes that not only is his body afflicted, but his very presence — his breath, his appearance — has become repugnant to his wife. This word emphasizes the radical isolation of the suffering righteous: rejected by his loved ones, he is alone in his trial.
H2114B.portee: This term reminds us that physical suffering often accompanies social rejection and loneliness. For the believer, it invites us not to judge the suffering one as impure or repugnant, but to surround them with compassion — just as Jesus approached the lepers rejected in His time.

sens: To apply force to compress, reduce the volume of a substance
To exert pressure to extract a liquid or material
To crush completely, reduce to powder or pulp
H2115.detail: 1. The verb zur denotes the action of pressing strongly, that is, applying force to compress something. When Gideon "presses" the wet fleece (Judges 6:38), he exerts continuous pressure to extract every drop of dew — the word evokes the gesture of twisting or squeezing to drain. 2. More broadly, to press means to crush, subject to destructive compression. Thus a foot that "crushes" (Job 39:18) or a beast that tramples completely reduces what it steps on. The image is that of a force that falls to annihilate or destroy. 3. In medical or physical contexts, the verb can describe the closing or healing of a wound — a wound that closes through compression or consolidation.
H2115.origine: The verb zur comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of pressure and compression. The initial image is that of a physical gesture: to press, twist, squeeze. This verb belongs to the family of Hebrew words related to compression and the action of reducing by force.
H2115.emploi: The verb zur appears mainly in concrete and poetic contexts. In Judges 6:38, Gideon presses the fleece of sheep to gather the dew and make water — a gesture from agricultural daily life. In Job 39:18, the poet speaks of feet that crush small creatures, an image of destruction. The verb is always used for a force acting on a material or object, never in an abstract or moral sense in these usages.
H2115.portee: This word invites the reader to feel the physical reality of the action: the gesture of the warrior Gideon who, with his hands, makes the dew flow, expresses his trust in God's power even in daily details. To press is also to transform — to draw something new from an ordinary material — and reminds us that God often acts through humble and simple means.

sens: that which is crushed, reduced to pieces
that which is broken, destroyed
H2116.detail:
1. A broken thing is literally something that has been crushed or reduced to fragments. In Isaiah 59:5, the prophet speaks of basilisk eggs: "if one is broken, a viper comes out." The image is that of a shell breaking, releasing its contents.
2. Figuratively, this word evokes any destruction, anything that is reduced to nothing. In this prophetic context, the plans of the wicked are compared to these fragile eggs: what seems solid and dangerous turns out to be hollow and perishable.
H2116.origine: The Hebrew word זוּרֶה (zurah) comes from a root expressing the action of reducing to pieces, grinding, or crushing. It is a feminine noun that designates the state of what has been broken, rather than the action itself. The family of words in Hebrew shares this idea of fragmentation and destruction.
H2116.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 59:5. The context is a prophetic description of the works of the wicked, compared to spider webs and serpent eggs. The prophet Isaiah uses this image to show the fragility and uselessness of evil plans: they may seem dangerous or complex (the webs), but they are as fragile as an eggshell.
H2116.portee: This word reminds us that projects built outside of God's will, no matter how clever or imposing they may seem, remain fundamentally fragile and mortal. It is a word of comfort for those who suffer under oppression: what threatens is in reality only chaff and an empty shell.

sens: son of Jonathan in the genealogy of Judah
H2117.detail: Zara is a man from the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:33. He is the son of Jonathan and the brother of Peleth, both descendants of Jerachmeel. He is a simple link in the genealogical chain of Israel, which shows the continuity of family lines during the time of the divided monarchy.
H2117.origine: The name Zara means "brightness" or "fullness" in Hebrew. It belongs to the same family of roots as other biblical names expressing brilliance or abundance, reflecting the importance given to the meanings of names in Hebrew culture.
H2117.emploi: Zara appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 2:33, in the genealogical record of Jerachmeel. He is among the many ancestors of Judah whose names the Bible preserves, without any particular account of his deeds or life. These genealogical lists affirm that all generations, even the less famous, are part of the history of God's people.

sens: to detach from an object to which one is fixed
to be displaced or dislocated
H2118.detail:
1. To detach from an object to which one is fixed: the breastplate (gold plate worn by the high priest on his chest) must not separate from the ephod (the priestly garment to which it was attached by a blue cord). This conveys the idea that two things joined together become disjoined. Exodus 28:28 and 39:21 emphasize that this separation must not occur, so that the breastplate remains firmly attached to the priest's garment during his service.
2. To be displaced or dislocated: the Hebrew verb expresses the movement of something that leaves its place or detaches from what held it. It is a physical and concrete notion, that of an involuntary displacement or the loosening of a connection.
H2118.origine: The Hebrew verb זָחַח (zakhakh) belongs to a small family of words related to the movement of separation or dislocation. The root evokes the idea that something detaches from where it was firmly held. It is a relatively rare action verb in the Bible, primarily used in the context of priestly worship to describe what must remain attached and not separate.
H2118.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Bible, in the two parallel passages of Exodus 28:28 and 39:21, which describe the same construction prescriptions for the high priest's breastplate. In both cases, the verb is used in the passive form (niphal): it is the breastplate that could be separated from the ephod — and indeed, that is what must not happen. The context is entirely cultic and liturgical: it is about ensuring that the priestly garment remains intact and that nothing dislocates during the sacred acts of Israel's worship.
H2118.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of stability and solidity in worship: every detail of the high priest's garment must be secure and well-attached, as service before God requires order and certainty. It is a lesson on attention to detail and faithfulness to God's instructions, even in material and seemingly minor matters.

sens: Animal that crawls and moves by undulating
Creeping creature, earth reptile
Figure of evil, cunning, and danger
H2119A.detail:
1. The word primarily designates an animal that moves by crawling, undulating along the ground: this is characteristic of snakes and reptiles. In Deuteronomy 32:24, God announces that He will send among the Israelites "the venom of serpents" as punishment, showing the dangerous creature in its venomous nature.
2. More broadly, it names any reptile that crawls on the earth, any creature that moves close to the ground. Micah 7:17 evokes enemies who "will lick the dust like a serpent, like the reptiles of the earth," using the image of the serpent to describe humiliation and submission.
3. The serpent symbolizes evil, cunning, and danger: an unpredictable, venomous animal that inspires fear. This is why it becomes a biblical image of sin and a threat to man.
H2119A.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of crawling, moving by undulating. The verb literally describes the characteristic movement of the serpent, which advances by twisting without using legs. It is a concrete word, derived from the observation of these creatures.
H2119A.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament. In both passages, it designates the serpent as a dangerous and repulsive creature. In Deuteronomy 32:24, it is among the plagues that God sends as punishment. In Micah 7:17, it serves as an image to express the humiliation of enemies who will have to crawl and lick the dust. In both cases, the serpent remains a threatening or despicable creature, never valued.
H2119A.portee: The serpent in Scripture is linked to the experience of evil and danger: it is an animal that man naturally fears, that injures and kills. Understanding this word helps to grasp how the Bible describes sin and its consequences. The serpent crawls, hides, strikes without warning: all traits that Scripture attributes to temptation and evil.

sens: To dread something or someone, to feel fear in the face of a threat or danger.
To hesitate out of respect or deference, to hold back one's words or actions for fear of disturbing or offending.
H2119B.detail: 1. To fear primarily means to be afraid in the face of a perceived threat: to dread evil, punishment, or danger. It is an emotional reaction to what is frightening, an apprehension of the heart. 2. The word also takes on the meaning of respecting out of fear, that is, to hold back one's words or actions out of regard for someone: Elihu, a young man facing elders, says "I feared" to let them know his feelings — he hesitated out of respect and deference for their authority (Job 32:6).
H2119B.origine: The root זחל evokes first the idea of retreating before danger, of withdrawing out of fear. The word is very rare in biblical Hebrew, where the more common verb יָרֵא (yareh) fulfills the primary role of expressing fear. The Aramaic דְּחַל (dehal) is its close Semitic equivalent and shares exactly this sense of fear or dread.
H2119B.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 32:6. Elihu, rising to speak, acknowledges that he "feared" to address the older and more experienced elders. His fear is not that of an immediate peril, but that of respect, of deference to the age and presumed wisdom of his interlocutors. The context shows a young man who hesitates, who holds back, then ultimately speaks up despite everything.
H2119B.portee: This word reminds us that fear can be a noble and measured feeling: respecting the experience and age of others, hesitating before speaking to avoid offending, is a form of wisdom. It is also a biblical reminder that recognizing our limits and legitimate concerns is not a weakness, but a mark of humility.

sens: Stone or place near Jerusalem
H2120.detail: 1. Zohéleth is a place near Jerusalem, identified as a stone or a spring. Its name means "serpent" in Hebrew, although the exact origin of this name is not clarified in the biblical text. This site was located near En-Roguel, another spring in the area, and served as a landmark for the inhabitants of Jerusalem (1 Kings 1:9).
H2120.origine: The Hebrew word זֹחֶלֶת (Zohéleth) derives from a root meaning "serpent" or "to glide" like a serpent. Its application to a place remains enigmatic: perhaps the terrain was winding, or the name evoked a geographical feature reminiscent of a serpent. This proper name has been preserved in biblical Hebrew without change, but its exact etymology is lost in the ancient history of Jerusalem.
H2120.emploi: Zohéleth appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 1:9. There, Adonijah, the son of King David, organizes a sacrifice and a political feast to rally the support of the powerful in the kingdom in order to be proclaimed king. The choice of this location, near En-Roguel and thus outside the royal city, perhaps suggests an attempt to hold the event away from the direct gaze of King David. This specific geographical site underscores the historical and documentary nature of the narrative.
H2120.portee: This passage illustrates how the geographical locations of the ancient Near East anchor biblical narratives in a concrete, non-mythical reality. For the modern reader, it serves as a reminder that the Bible speaks of real places and real political events — here, a succession struggle within the Davidic royal house that will have lasting consequences for the people of Israel.

sens: That moves with violence and passion
That manifests pride or arrogance
H2121.detail:
1. Impetuous describes something that moves with force and turbulence, without restraint: the image is that of waves that rage and would overwhelm everything in their path. In Psalm 124:5, the "impetuous waves" symbolize the waves of distress and danger that would have swallowed the people of Israel without divine protection — it is the very violence of nature unleashed.
2. The word can also evoke the haughty and arrogant attitude of one who imposes themselves by brute force, without fear or respect: a brutal, aggressive pride, an insolence that nothing restrains.
H2121.origine: The Hebrew word זֵידוֹן (zedon) comes from a root that expresses overflow, rise, excess. It belongs to a family of words evoking pride and presumption: one who "rises" above others, who elevates themselves against the established order. This root paints the image of a force that grows, swells, and does not accept limits.
H2121.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Psalm 124:5. It characterizes the tumultuous waters that would have engulfed Israel. The context is clearly one of natural threat or persecution: the "impetuous waves" represent the brute power of enemies or trials. The term depicts an irresistible, thoughtless force, without control — whether it be that of floodwaters or human pride.
H2121.portee: This word reminds the reader that brute power — whether from events, enemies, or our own passions — does not have the final say. God can stop even what seems irresistible. In the face of the impetuous waves of life, the believer learns not to fear but to trust in the one who masters the elements.

sens: Brightness, luminous brilliance of a thing or person
Magnificence, glory, sovereign dignity
Aspect of the face, complexion
To pale, change color (in the sense of losing its brightness)
H2122.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the brilliant and resplendent shine that a thing projects. In Nebuchadnezzar's vision, the colossal statue shines with extraordinary splendor (Daniel 2:31): it conveys the image of something that impresses by its radiance and magnificence.
2. The word then evokes glory, honor, and royal power — what makes a king venerable and splendid in the eyes of his subjects. Nebuchadnezzar covers "his glory of my kingdom, my magnificence and my splendor" (Daniel 4:36): it is all that adorns him and makes him majestic.
3. In the context of the face and complexion, the word denotes the bright and healthy appearance of the face. The queen asks the king: "Let not your face change color" (Daniel 5:10), referring to this natural brightness of the complexion.
4. By extension, "to change splendor" or "to change color" means to pale, to lose that brightness of the face — a sign of fear or deep trouble. When Daniel sees the heavenly vision, he "changes color" (Daniel 7:28), overwhelmed by fear.
H2122.origine: The Hebrew word זִיו (ziv) belongs to a family of words related to brightness and light. It is close to the root that evokes what shines, radiates, or glows. In Aramaic (the language of some passages in Daniel), it takes on the meaning of visible light, brilliance, or complexion — what is seen and observed by the eye.
H2122.emploi: This word appears six times in Hebrew and Aramaic, exclusively in the book of Daniel. It is used to describe the splendor of the prophetic statue (2:31) and the restored glory of Nebuchadnezzar (4:36); it also designates the complexion of the face (5:10) and the change of color due to fear (5:6, 5:9, 7:28). The context is always that of the visible manifestation of power or emotion — what is seen and strikes the eye.
H2122.portee: This word reminds us that the glory and power of the world — statues, thrones, royal magnificence — are merely brilliant appearances, while true dignity is in God. It also shows that the fear of the Lord makes human pride pale: the change of color of the face becomes a sign of the awareness of the divine that abolishes the vain splendor of man.

sens: wild animal that moves freely in nature
that which belongs to God and falls under His domain
H2123A.detail:
1. The word ziz refers to living creatures that move — animals. It is a generic term for all beings that move, that have the ability to move by themselves in fields and mountains. In Psalm 50:11, the psalmist says: "I know all the birds of the mountains, and everything that moves in the fields belongs to me" — the word here refers to creatures that roam the wild spaces.
2. These moving creatures are the property of God. They fall under the divine domain, under the governance of the One who created them and knows them. In Psalm 80:14, the "beast of the field" that ravages the vineyard represents the plagues that God allows. The word evokes not only the concrete animal but also the idea that every living creature, everything that has the ability to move, depends on God and responds to His order.
H2123A.origine: The word ziz comes from a root expressing movement and agitation. It is linked to the image of dynamism, mobility. The word appears mainly in the poetry and wisdom texts of the Old Testament to designate mobile creatures, in contrast to immobile beings or plants. The root evokes what moves, what flutters or stirs.
H2123A.emploi: The word ziz appears only twice in the Psalms. In Psalm 50:11, it describes the creatures that populate the fields and mountains — a living and dynamic world that God knows and possesses. In Psalm 80:14, it designates the "beasts" (the wild boar and animals of the fields) that ravage the vineyard. In both contexts, the word emphasizes the existence of autonomous creatures, with their own mobility, but which remain under the control or permission of God.
H2123A.portee: This word reminds the reader that all of creation — every moving creature — belongs to God. It invites us to contemplate the living world not as chaos, but as an ordered whole, known and governed by the One who sustains it. Meditating on this term brings us closer to a biblical vision: even wild beasts are not outside of God's plan.

sens: complete and generous abundance
that which completely fills and satisfies the heart
the total richness of something in all its strength
H2123B.detail: 1. The word describes an abundance that lacks nothing, a generous fullness: the text of Isaiah 66:11 speaks of "the fullness of His glory," meaning the glory of God in all its richness and fullness, like a mother's breast that nourishes abundantly. 2. It is also that which fills and deeply satisfies: in this same passage, believers savor this fullness with joy, like someone tasting food that completely fulfills and satisfies beyond what they hoped for.
H2123B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of sufficiency and overflowing. It is rare in the Old Testament — known to occur only once — and carries the image of a wealth that is not held back, offered generously. It is a word that breathes maternal abundance and complete satisfaction.
H2123B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 66:11. It carries a highly poetic and comforting charge: it refers to the fullness of divine glory that believers will enjoy, nourished like children at the breast of God's comfort. The context is that of divine comfort offered after affliction, hence the emphasis on a generous and limitless abundance.
H2123B.portee: This word invites the believer to contemplate not only sufficiency but the superabundance of God's glory. It reminds that God does not give sparingly, but offers a fullness that fills the heart — a tender maternal image of the Father who nourishes His children not only with what they need but with what satisfies them with joy.

sens: Chief of the tribe of Simeon during the divided monarchy
H2124G.detail: Ziza is a Simeonite chief known only by a mention in the genealogies of the first Book of Chronicles. He lived during the time of the divided monarchy, when the kingdom of Israel was split into two: the Northern Kingdom (Israel) and the Southern Kingdom (Judah). His name appears in the genealogical list of the descendants of Simeon, where he is presented as the son of Schipheï and holds a position of responsibility among his people (1 Chronicles 4:37).
H2124G.origine: The name Ziza means "shining" or "splendid" in Hebrew. It comes from a root expressing brightness and luminosity, a common image in biblical names to express glory, dignity, or distinction. This name reflects the importance of this man in his tribe.
H2124G.emploi: Ziza is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:37, in the genealogy of the Simeonites. This unique mention places him within a lineage of tribal leaders during the time of the divided monarchy. The genealogical context shows that he represented an important branch of the tribe of Simeon and contributed to maintaining the organization of the people during this period in Israel's history.

sens: Son of Rehoboam and Maacah
Prince of Judah during the divided monarchy
H2124H.detail:
1. Ziza is a son of King Rehoboam and Maacah, the daughter of Absalom. He is mentioned in 2 Chronicles 11:20 among the children of Rehoboam, alongside his brothers Abijah, Attai, and his sister Shelomith. He lived during the time of the division of the kingdom between Judah and Israel, in the 10th century BCE.
2. As a son of a king of Judah, Ziza belonged to the royal family and enjoyed the status of prince. His name means "shining" or "resplendent," reflecting the importance of his royal lineage in the history of Israel.
H2124H.origine: The name Ziza comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to shine" or "to radiate." This name was given to express brightness or brilliance, perhaps in reference to the dignity and nobility expected of a king's child. The name evokes the idea of a remarkable and distinguished figure.
H2124H.emploi: Ziza is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 11:20. He is presented there as one of the sons that Rehoboam had with Maacah, the daughter of Absalom. This passage lists several of his legitimate children, thus establishing the royal genealogy of Judah and Ziza's place in the dynastic succession of the southern kingdom.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Gershon, son of Shimei
Second son of Shimei after Jachath
H2125.detail:
1. Zina is a Levite belonging to the family of the Gershonites, descendants of Levi through Gershon. He is the son of Shimei, mentioned during the census of the Levites under King David (1 Chronicles 23:10).
2. Among the four sons of Shimei, Zina held the rank of second son: Jachath was the chief, and Zina the second (1 Chronicles 23:11). Although Jeush and Beriah, his two other brothers, did not have many sons, all four formed together a single paternal house in the census of the Levites.
H2125.origine: The name Zina means "abundance" in Hebrew. It is a name that expresses the idea of fullness and richness. In 1 Chronicles 23:10, he is also called Zizah, which could be a variant of the same name or another form of his official designation.
H2125.emploi: Zina appears twice in the biblical text, always in the context of the census of the Levites ordered by King David. He is presented as one of the sons of Shimei, from the lineage of Gershon, one of the three major families of Levites (along with Kohath and Merari). His role was to participate in the organization and service of the Tabernacle, alongside his brothers. He receives no other particular mention in Scripture, making him a minor but attested figure of the Israelite priestly hierarchy.

sens: man of the tribe of Gad during the divided monarchy
H2127.detail: Zia is a man belonging to the tribe of Gad, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. He lived during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two distinct kingdoms. He is the son of Abihail and the brother of Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jacan, and Eber. Zia is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:13, in a genealogical list of family leaders of the tribe of Gad who lived in Bashan.
H2127.origine: The name Zia means "tumult" or "agitation" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking noise or movement. It is a simple and short name, borne by this man of Gad without the Bible recounting more about his life or actions.
H2127.emploi: Zia appears only once in Scripture: in 1 Chronicles 5:13. He is cited among the family leaders of Gad who lived in the region of Bashan, east of the Jordan. This mention is part of a genealogical enumeration intended to document the lineages of the tribes of Israel after the return from exile. No events of his life, no particular acts are reported; he is simply identified as a member of an important family of his tribe.

sens: City of southern Judah
H2128G.detail: Ziph is a city that was located in the south of Judah, between Ithnan and Thelem, in the region that God assigned to the tribe of Judah. It appears in the list of cities of Judah enumerated in chapter 15 of the book of Joshua (Joshua 15:24).
H2128G.origine: The name Ziph literally means "battlement" or "entrenchment," perhaps evoking a fortified or defended city. It is a Hebrew toponym, that is, the name of a place.
H2128G.emploi: Ziph appears only once in the Bible, in the list of cities assigned to the tribe of Judah at the time of the division of the promised land under Joshua's leadership. It is mentioned between Ithnan and Thelem, indicating its location in the southern region.

sens: fortified city of Judah, southeast of Hebron
H2128H.detail: Ziph is a city located in Judah, in the mountainous region southeast of Hebron, between Carmel and Juttah. It is mentioned as one of the cities in the territory of Judah in the geographical register of Joshua 15:55. Ziph is best known as the place where David took refuge to escape from Saul's pursuit: the "desert of Ziph" or the "mountain of the desert of Ziph" (1 Samuel 23:14-15) served as a refuge for David and his men, a rocky and hard-to-access area where Saul, despite his army of three thousand warriors, could not reach him (1 Samuel 26:2).
H2128H.origine: The name Ziph comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of "fortress" or "battlement." The inhabitants of Ziph were called the Ziphites (Ziphis in Hebrew). The city owed its importance to its strategic position in the heights of Judah.
H2128H.emploi: Ziph is mentioned five times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the historical books. It first appears in the list of cities of Judah (Joshua 15:55). It became especially famous during David's flight from Saul: the desert of Ziph is the scene of three episodes of pursuit (1 Samuel 23:14-15 and 26:2), where Saul descends with his army to seek David, but God protects His servant by preserving him from capture. The place is presented as a mountainous and uninhabited region, ideal terrain for hiding.
H2128H.portee: The story of David at Ziph illustrates how God protects those He chooses, even in the midst of danger and persecution. It is a place of trust: while Saul has superior military forces, David finds refuge in these remote mountains and is never delivered into the hands of his enemy, despite repeated searches. For the Christian reader, Ziph symbolizes the refuge that God offers to His children in times of trial.

sens: Descendant de Juda et fils de Mareshah
Fortified city in southern Judah
H2128I.detail:
1. Ziph is a man from the tribe of Judah, son of Mareshah and brother of Jerachmeel, mentioned genealogically in 1 Chronicles 2:42. He belonged to the lineage of Caleb and lived during the time of the divided monarchy.
2. Ziph also refers to a fortified city located in southern Judah, between Carmel and Juttah, near Hebron. It appears in the list of cities that King Rehoboam built to defend his kingdom (2 Chronicles 11:8).
H2128I.origine: The name Ziph comes from Hebrew and literally means "machicolation" or "battlement" — a structure projecting from the top of a fortification. This figurative meaning applies either to an ancestor of the lineage or to the fortified city that bears its name, both linked to the region of Judah.
H2128I.emploi: Ziph appears twice in the Bible. First as a genealogical figure in 1 Chronicles 2:42, where he is listed among the descendants of Caleb. Then, it refers to a city of Judah mentioned in 2 Chronicles 11:8 in the list of fortifications that Rehoboam built to strengthen the defense of his kingdom after the schism. The proximity of the personal name and the city suggests that the man and the place are historically linked.

sens: Son of Jehalléel, from the tribe of Judah, during the time of the divided monarchy
City in southern Judah, between Ithnan and Telem
City of Judah, southeast of Hebron, between Carmel and Jutta
H2128J.detail:
1. Ziph is a man from the tribe of Judah, son of Jehalléel (1 Chronicles 4:16), living during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. He had three brothers: Zipha, Tiria, and Asareel. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the genealogy of the descendants of Judah.
2. Ziph is also the name of a city in southern Judah, located between the cities of Ithnan and Telem, in the lowlands of the south.
3. Ziph also refers to another city of Judah, situated in the heights southeast of Hebron, between Carmel and Jutta, in the mountainous district of Judah. This locality is probably where David took refuge while fleeing from King Saul.
H2128J.origine: The name Ziph means "battlements" or "crest," referring to a prominent geographical feature — probably the rocky bastions or fortifications of a city. Several cities and characters bear this name in the Bible, as it is common for places to be named after landscape features or for families to give their descendants the name of a city of origin.
H2128J.emploi: Ziph appears only once in the preserved biblical texts as a living person: in 1 Chronicles 4:16, where he is cited in the genealogy of the sons of Jehalléel, one of the direct descendants of Judah. This brief mention tells us nothing about his life, deeds, or historical role. However, the name Ziph, more broadly, is associated with important places in the history of Judah, especially during the period of the divided monarchy, where these cities played a role in the geography and defense of the southern kingdom.

sens: Man from the tribe of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy
H2129.detail: Zipha is a man from the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Jehalléleel and the brother of Ziph, Tiria, and Asareel. His name appears in the genealogy of Judah listed in 1 Chronicles 4:16, among the descendants of this important tribe.
H2129.origine: The name Zipha literally means "battlements" or "rampart" — an image drawn from the architecture of fortifications, where battlements are the openings at the top of the walls. It is a typical Hebrew name from the biblical period, formed from a root that evokes protection and defense. Zipha shares its etymology with his brother Ziph (H2128), whose name is similar.
H2129.emploi: Zipha appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:16, in a genealogical list of the descendants of Judah. He is presented exclusively by his lineage (son of Jehalléleel) and his brotherly ties with three other men from his family. No events of his life, no actions are reported: only his existence and his place in the genealogy of Judah are attested.

sens: Inhabitants of the region of Ziph, in Judah
H2130.detail: 1. The Ziphiens are the inhabitants of the region of Ziph, a mountainous area in southern Judah. They appear in the story as the informers against David when he was fleeing from King Saul: "The Ziphiens went up to Saul at Gibeah, and said: Is not David hiding on the hill of Hakilah?" (1 Samuel 26:1). They denounced David twice, revealing his hiding places.
H2130.origine: The name "Ziphiens" comes from Ziph, the name of their city or region of origin in Judah. These inhabitants bore the name of their land, according to a common practice in ancient Israel. The term appears only in the accounts of David's flight.
H2130.emploi: The Ziphiens appear three times in the Old Testament, all three accounts concerning David. In 1 Samuel 23:19, they go to Saul to denounce him. In 1 Samuel 26:1, they do so again. Psalm 54, titled "A Psalm of David, when the Ziphiens came to say to Saul," is a prayer of David in the face of this betrayal. Their name remains attached to this act of betrayal.
H2130.portee: The story of the Ziphiens reminds the reader that David, although anointed by God to be king, had to endure deceit and betrayal. It shows God's faithfulness to His servant despite human threats and invites the Christian to pray as David did, entrusting his difficult circumstances to God rather than seeking vengeance.

sens: Fiery projectile or arrow launched as a weapon
Flame or burning fire that burns and consumes
H2131A.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a formidable weapon: a fiery dart or arrow that the warrior launches against his enemy. In Proverbs 26:18, the one who deceives his friend and then cries out, "I was joking!" is compared to a madman who shoots flames and arrows bringing death — the image emphasizes the deadly danger of lying.
2. More broadly, it evokes the burning fire, the flame that burns and consumes. In Isaiah 50:11, God addresses those who light a fire of rebellion and arm themselves with torches: He warns them that the flames they have ignited will burn them themselves, and they will lie down in pain. The image shifts from the projectile to the destructive fire that falls back on the one who provoked it.
H2131A.origine: The Hebrew word זֵק (ziq) likely comes from a root expressing the brightness or liveliness of fire. It belongs to a family of terms describing fiery and luminous phenomena: the fire that bursts forth, the flame that dances. This image of the fiery projectile was very concrete in ancient wars, where warriors launched fiery darts or brands against enemy walls and troops.
H2131A.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In both instances, it carries a dramatic and destructive charge. In Proverbs 26:18, it illustrates the ravages of lying and deception — an act seemingly light but which wounds mortally. In Isaiah 50:11, it symbolizes rebellion against God and the ensuing judgment: the one who relies on their own fires instead of walking in the light of God will be consumed. In both cases, the word evokes an immediate danger and inevitable destruction.
H2131A.portee: This image of the fiery torch challenges the believer regarding the consequences of their actions, particularly deception and rebellion. Just as the fiery arrow falls back on the one who shoots it, our lying words and rebellious choices against God burn and wound us. Isaiah 50:11 invites us to seek the authentic light of God rather than feeding our own fires — an exhortation to obedience and trust.

sens: iron link that imprisons or restrains someone
captivity, servitude
state of one who is subjected to the power of a conqueror
H2131B.detail:
1. A chain is a material object, made of interlinked metal rings, that is placed on the ankles or wrists of a prisoner to prevent escape. It symbolizes physical imprisonment: in Psalms 149:8, enemies' kings are "bound" with chains, meaning they are captured and rendered powerless.
2. The word also evokes captivity itself, the state of slavery or servitude imposed by an external force. In Nahum 3:10, the nobles of Nineveh are "loaded with chains" to signify that they become prisoners of war, transported as spoils of the victor.
3. Figuratively, the chain represents subjugation and domination: in Isaiah 45:14, the defeated peoples walk "in chains" before the people of God, meaning in a position of humiliation and complete submission.
H2131B.origine: The Hebrew word ziq comes from a root that evokes the action of tightening, enclosing. It is a concrete word, primarily designating the metallic object itself. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), it is translated by Greek words denoting chains or fetters. The word belongs to the vocabulary of wars and punishments: it describes what immobilizes and enslaves.
H2131B.emploi: The word appears four times in the Old Testament, always to describe a reality of imprisonment or captivity. In Job 36:8, it refers to chains of adversity into which one may fall. In Psalms 149:8, the chains are the concrete instrument of God's people's victory over their enemies. In Isaiah 45:14 and Nahum 3:10, the word takes on a collective dimension: entire crowds of the defeated are "chained," marked by the seal of defeat and submission to the victor. The context is always one of power, judgment, and captivity.
H2131B.portee: This word reminds the biblical reader of the reality of sin as slavery: just as a chain physically restrains a prisoner, sin chains the soul. It also evokes God's victory over His enemies and His power to impose His order: when the Word speaks of "chains," it shows the cost of rebellion and the triumph of divine justice. For the believer, this word invites reflection on their own freedom in Christ and the power of divine judgment.

sens: tree producing olives, with gray and evergreen leaves, very common in the Holy Land
the mountain covered with olive trees near Jerusalem, a symbolic place of suffering and hope
H2132G.detail:
1. The olive tree is the characteristic tree of the Mediterranean basin, known in the Holy Land for its fruit, the olive, and its precious oil. It is a robust tree that can live for a very long time and symbolizes blessing and peace in the Bible. The Hebrew word designates both the tree and the place where it grows.

2. The Mount of Olives is a hill that borders Jerusalem to the east. It is where King David fled weeping during Absalom's rebellion (2 Samuel 15:30), showing this place as one of crisis and affliction. The prophet Zechariah also sees it as a sign of the end times: the day when the Lord's feet will stand on this mountain to split it and accomplish salvation (Zechariah 14:4).
H2132G.origine: The Hebrew word zaït comes from a very ancient root that designates the olive tree. In Greek, this place is called Élaiôn (ἐλαιών), which comes from the same meaning: "place of olives." The word evokes the simple and concrete image of the tree that dominates the Palestinian landscape, familiar to every inhabitant of Jerusalem.
H2132G.emploi: The word appears twice in the Segond, always in the plural to designate the mountain rather than the isolated tree. In 2 Samuel 15:30, it is the scene of King David's painful departure fleeing from his rebellious son: he ascends the Mount of Olives weeping. In Zechariah 14:4, the Mount of Olives becomes a major prophetic place where God will intervene at the end of times. These two usages show the transition from the concrete (a real geographical location) to the symbolic (a sign of divine intervention).
H2132G.portee: The Mount of Olives reminds the reader that God remains present in the midst of suffering and distress, as He showed during King David's flight. It also announces that the Lord will act to save His people and transform the world. This geographical place becomes a landmark of biblical hope.

sens: The tree that produces olives, with its evergreen leaves and small white flowers
The fruit of this tree, used to extract oil
The oil extracted from olives, essential for cooking and worship rituals
An image of blessing, prosperity, and peace
The Mount of Olives, to the east of Jerusalem
H2132H.detail: 1. The olive tree is the emblematic tree of the Mediterranean, with gray-green leaves and small oval fruits. Noah's dove returns with a plucked olive branch, a sign that the waters of the flood have receded (Genesis 8:11) — the tree itself symbolizes the return to life. 2. Olives are the fruits of this tree, harvested by beating the branches: the children, widows, and the poor had the right to glean afterwards (Deuteronomy 24:20), as the harvest was abundant. 3. Olive oil fueled the lamps of the temple — the Lord requests pure oil for the lampstands (Exodus 27:20) — and was used in priestly anointings and worship perfumes (Exodus 30:24). 4.
