The flourishing olive tree, with its branches laden with fruit, becomes an image of the prosperous and blessed righteous: "I am like a flourishing olive tree in the house of God" (Psalms 52:10); it is a tree of peace, whose orchards were destroyed in times of war to starve the enemy (Judges 15:5). 5. The Mount of Olives, or Olive Mountain, is the mountain that overlooks Jerusalem from the east, where Jesus prayed before His Passion.
H2132H.origine: The Hebrew word zaït comes from an ancient root meaning probably "greenness" or "foliage." The olive tree is the quintessential Mediterranean tree, cultivated in Israel since antiquity: Deuteronomy lists it among the seven crops of the promised land, along with wheat, barley, vine, fig, pomegranate, and date (Deuteronomy 8:8). Its name also gave rise in Hebrew to the Mount of Olives (Har HaZeïtim in modern Hebrew).
H2132H.emploi: The word zaït appears 34 times in the Old Testament, mainly in agricultural, ritual, and symbolic contexts. The tree itself: the olive tree is a gift from God to the promised people (Joshua 24:13 — God gives them orchards they did not plant) and a possession that should not be destroyed without reason (Deuteronomy 20:19 — you shall not cut down fruit trees). The oil: it is the oil for the lamps of the sanctuary (Exodus 27:20) and for anointings, particularly that of the king and priest. The fruit: the harvests can be destroyed in divine judgment (Amos 4:9, Micah 6:15). The image: the flourishing olive tree symbolizes the happiness and stability of the righteous in Psalms 52:10 and 128:3; the broken or stripped olive tree expresses misfortune and barrenness (Job 15:33, Jeremiah 11:16).
H2132H.portee: The olive tree reminds the reader that God generously provides for the needs of His people — oil was food, medicine, and a symbol of the Holy Spirit in Christian thought. Its cultivation requires patience and waiting, as the olive tree only enters abundant production after years: it is a lesson on trust and the duration of commitment. The destruction of the olive tree in judgment teaches that even material blessings depend on obedience. For the Christian, the olive tree also becomes an image of stable life in grace (Romans 11 will speak of the cultivated olive tree and the grafted branches, symbolizing Israel and the nations).

sens: man of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Bilhan
H2133.detail: Zethan is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned only once in the Bible as the son of Bilhan. He appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Jediael, alongside his brothers Jeusch, Benjamin, Ehud, Kenaana, Tarsis, and Achishachar (1 Chronicles 7:10). His name means "olive" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking stability or fertility. He lived during the time of the divided monarchy, but the Bible does not report any particular events from his life.
H2133.origine: The name Zethan comes from the Hebrew זֵיתָן and literally means "olive." It is formed from זַיִת (zaït), the word for the olive tree, an important fruit tree in Israel. This name reveals the importance of the olive tree in biblical culture and economy: a symbol of peace, wealth, and divine blessing.
H2133.emploi: Zethan appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:10, in the genealogical record of the tribe of Benjamin. He is presented there as the son of Bilhan and brother to six other men. This mention is part of the enumeration of the Benjaminite family heads and their sons, made to establish tribal lines of descent. No other details are given about his role or actions.

sens: without mixture, without material impurity
without moral or spiritual defect
just, innocent, upright before God
H2134.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes physical purity, without mixture or dirt: pure olive oil (Exodus 27:20) or pure incense (Exodus 30:34) that God requires for worship, showing that God desires the best and most refined for His service.
2. By extension, it characterizes a person whose heart, intentions, or conduct are free from malice or guilt: Job asserts "my way is pure" (Job 11:4), meaning without reproach, without deviation, without fraud.
3. In moral and religious language, it designates one who is upright before God, innocent of guilt, whose actions and thoughts are just and conform to divine justice, as expressed by Job in Job 33:9 when he speaks of one who is pure in his ways.
H2134.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of clarity, brightness, of that which shines. The word belongs to the lexical field of cultic and moral purity in Israel. It stands in opposition to what is defiled, impure, or mixed. The same word can describe pure gold, pure incense, or a pure heart, showing that in biblical thought, physical purity and moral purity are strongly linked: one reflects the other.
H2134.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the prescriptions of Leviticus and Exodus regarding worship (pure oil, pure incense for the lampstand and the showbread: Exodus 27:20, 30:34; Leviticus 24:2, 24:7), where it emphasizes that only the best is worthy to be offered to God. It is also used by the sages in Proverbs and Job to qualify the moral uprightness or innocence of a person (Job 8:6, 11:4, 16:17, 33:9; Proverbs 16:2, 20:11, 21:8), where it carries the meaning of "just" or "innocent." In these sapiential contexts, it expresses the conviction that the purity of heart and uprightness of life are known and appreciated by God.
H2134.portee: This word teaches that God requires purity, both in worship and in moral life. The emphasis on pure oil and pure incense in worship reveals that God does not accept a careless or degraded offering. On a personal level, the call to be pure and just reminds the believer that God sees the heart and honors those whose soul is upright, inviting them to a life without duplicity or malice.

sens: free from moral stain or guilt
without sin or blame
made clean or innocent
to purify oneself
H2135.detail:
1. To be pure means to be free from guilt or moral stain — to have a clear conscience before God. Job and his friends pose the anguished question: "How can a man be pure before God?" (Job 25:4), acknowledging that no one can boast of absolute innocence.
2. The word also denotes the absence of blame or defect in divine judgment: the psalmist declares that God will be just without blame in His sentence (Psalms 51:6), meaning that He can be reproached for neither falsehood nor injustice.
3. To purify one's heart or path means to make them clean and innocent, often through conversion and adherence to the Word. The psalmist asks how a young man will make his path pure: "by keeping it according to Your word" (Psalms 119:9).
H2135.origine: The verb zakah comes from a root evoking clarity and the absence of trouble. It belongs to the family of words expressing cleanliness and righteousness. In Hebrew, it is linked to the idea of brightness — what is pure shines, while what is stained becomes darkened. The word refers to ritual and moral purity, a purification that makes a person worthy to stand before God.
H2135.emploi: This verb appears 8 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms and the Book of Job. It is first used in the absolute sense: to be pure (Job 15:14; Job 25:4). It also denotes the action of purifying, making pure — the heart (Psalms 73:13), the path (Psalms 119:9), or oneself (Proverbs 20:9). The word carries a strong theological dimension: people wonder if it is possible to be pure before God, introducing the theme of grace and forgiveness. In this context, purity is not merely an external observance but an inner transformation.
H2135.portee: This word invites the believer to take seriously the purity before God — not an unattainable perfection, but a sincerity of heart and obedience to His Word. It also reminds that no man can justify himself by his works, which opens the door to divine grace and, for the Christian, to forgiveness in Christ.

sens: State of one who has not committed the fault or crime of which he is accused
Moral purity and integrity before God
Absence of guilt in the eyes of the law and justice
H2136.detail:
1. Innocence is the fact of not having committed the reprehensible act of which one is accused. Daniel affirms this before King Darius: he has violated no decree, thus he is innocent of the false accusation against him (Daniel 6:22).
2. It is also the purity of heart and conduct before God: a state of inner righteousness, not just the formal absence of guilt. To be innocent before God means to have a clear conscience and to live according to His will.
3. More broadly, innocence denotes the position of one who does not deserve punishment: neither rightly accused nor guilty in the eyes of divine justice. This is why God can justify the innocent and protect him, as He does for Daniel by shutting the mouths of the lions.
H2136.origine: The Hebrew word zakhou comes from a root that primarily means "to be pure, to be clean." This idea of purity naturally extends to the notion of innocence: the one who is innocent is one whose guilt has not tarnished moral purity. The family of the word includes terms related to justification and purity in divine judgment.
H2136.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 6:22. It is a moment of maximum stakes: Daniel is falsely accused of transgressing a decree of the king and risks death in the lions' den. By declaring his innocence, he affirms that his conscience is clear before God and before the king. This is why God miraculously saves him: Daniel's innocence justifies divine intervention. This term emphasizes that the innocence of the righteous is visible in the eyes of God and can be established by miracle.
H2136.portee: This word from Daniel reminds believers that innocence — the purity of conscience before God — has real spiritual value. Even when unjustly accused or in danger, those who have walked uprightly can count on God's justice. It is a model of trust in the face of persecution: not fearing men when one can affirm their integrity before the Lord.

sens: transparent and shiny material, hard and fragile, obtained by melting sand
precious and rare substance in antiquity
luxury and beauty object
H2137.detail:
1. Glass is a transparent and shiny material made by heating sand. It is a hard but fragile substance that breaks easily. In Job 28:17, glass is mentioned for its clarity and brilliance: the text states that wisdom cannot be compared to gold or glass, nor exchanged for a fine gold vessel.
2. In antiquity, glass was a very rare and precious material, thus very expensive. This is why the Bible refers to it as an object of great value, alongside gold and noble metals. Making a glass vessel was a feat of ancient craftsmanship.
3. Glass symbolizes rarity, delicacy, and beauty. By mentioning it alongside fine gold, the biblical text shows that true wisdom surpasses in value all material treasures, even the most beautiful and rare.
H2137.origine: The Hebrew word זְכוּכִית likely comes from a root meaning "to shine" or "to be transparent." It is a specifically Hebrew word, without simple equivalents in other ancient Semitic languages. It denotes glass in its most literal sense: the substance obtained by melting, characterized by its transparency and brilliance.
H2137.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 28:17. It is found in a passage where Job enumerates the treasures and riches of the world to affirm that wisdom surpasses them all. Glass is cited alongside fine gold and other precious materials, reflecting its status as a rare and costly good in the ancient world. This unique occurrence shows that glass was a known reality in Israel, likely through trade or contact with neighboring civilizations that mastered its production.
H2137.portee: Meditating on this passage helps the believer to relativize the value of material wealth, even the most beautiful and rare. Wisdom — the kind that God alone possesses and offers to those who seek it — is worth infinitely more than all earthly treasures. This invites a reorientation of our priorities: to seek first the wisdom of God rather than the accumulation of goods, however precious they may be.

sens: male person
adult or adolescent man (as opposed to women and children)
H2138.detail:
1. The word simply designates a person of the male sex, in contrast to the female. It is the natural term for speaking of boys or men depending on the context.
2. In the provided biblical texts, it specifically refers to the adult or adolescent man capable of participating in public life — notably in religious festivals (Exodus 23:17 and Deuteronomy 16:16, where all males must present themselves before the Lord) or in wars (Deuteronomy 20:13). It is a term that marks the responsibility and social engagement of the one who bears it.
H2138.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "male, virile" and opposes the female (nebeha). It does not simply designate a biological sex, but recognizes the specific place of the male in the family and public structures of Israel.
H2138.emploi: The word appears four times in the Torah, always in the plural ("the males"). The first three occurrences (Exodus 23:17, Exodus 34:23, Deuteronomy 16:16) concern the obligation for all males of Israel to present themselves before the Lord at the three great festivals — which shows that only the male sex is recognized as responsible for public religious duties. The last occurrence (Deuteronomy 20:13) designates the men liable to death in war, thus distinguishing the males (targeted by the sword) from women and children. Each context reveals how the status of "male" engages public, religious, or military responsibility.
H2138.portee: This word reminds us that in the Old Testament, official religious responsibilities were reserved for men, reflecting the structures of the time — without teaching a hierarchy of the sexes before God. For the Christian reader, it invites examination of how the New Testament, particularly through the Holy Spirit, liberates access to spiritual life beyond these distinctions (Galatians 3:28).

sens: father of Shammua, one of the twelve spies sent to explore Canaan
H2139G.detail: 1. Zaccur is the father of Shammua, who represents the tribe of Reuben among the twelve men sent by Moses to explore the promised land (Numbers 13:4). He is mentioned only once in the Bible, solely to identify his son.
H2139G.origine: The name Zaccur means "he who remembers" or "memorable," derived from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of memory and remembrance. It is a common theophoric name in Israel, reminding that God remembers His people.
H2139G.emploi: Zaccur appears only once in the scriptures, in Numbers 13:4, where he is presented as the father of Shammua. The Bible provides no further information about him. His name is preserved only because his son was chosen for this crucial exploration mission, which proved pivotal for Israel's history in the wilderness.

sens: Man of the tribe of Simeon during the divided monarchy
H2139H.detail: Zaccur is a man of the tribe of Simeon mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:26. He appears in the genealogy of the family of Mishma, presented as the son of Hammuel and the father of Shimei. He lived during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two rival kingdoms (the Northern Kingdom and the Southern Kingdom).
H2139H.origine: The name Zaccur means "he who remembers" or "memorialized," coming from the Hebrew root zakar which means "to remember." This root is very common in biblical Hebrew and expresses the idea of keeping in memory, of not forgetting. The name reflects the importance of memory and transmission in Israelite culture, particularly in genealogies where each name is a trace of the remembrance of ancestors.
H2139H.emploi: Zaccur is a minor figure in the tribal genealogies of Israel. He is mentioned only once in 1 Chronicles 4:26, within the list of descendants of Simeon. The Bible identifies him simply by his place in the genealogical chain: son of Hammuel, father of Shimei. This type of genealogical mention served to document the families and lineages of the tribes of Israel after the Exile.
H2139H.portee: Zaccur reminds us that even the most discreet biblical figures — those barely mentioned in the text — are part of God's people and His history. His name, which means "memorialized," invites the reader to reflect on how God remembers His people, regardless of the apparent importance or forgetfulness of a person in the eyes of the world.

sens: Levite son of Jaaziah, brother of Shoham and Ibri
H2139I.detail: Zaccur is a Levite of the tribe of Levi, living during the time of the divided monarchy. He is the son of Jaaziah and the brother of Shoham and Ibri, all three members of the priestly family of Merari. His name appears in the genealogical register of the descendants of Merari recorded by the Chronicler to establish the temple service (1 Chronicles 24:27). Although little known, he is part of the lineage of Levites responsible for worship in the Jerusalem temple.
H2139I.origine: The name Zaccur means "he who remembers" or "memorial," coming from the Hebrew root that expresses the idea of remembering or making memory. This root evokes the importance of remembrance and faithfulness in the biblical tradition. The name carried a religious significance, reminding that God remembers His covenant and that His people must do so as well.
H2139I.emploi: Zaccur appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 24:27. This is a genealogical mention, part of the records that the Chronicler compiles to document the organization of Levitical families during the time of the divided monarchy. This list served to establish the responsibilities of the cultic service in the temple. The genealogical context indicates that he was an important Levite in the history of temple service.

sens: son of Asaph, Levitical musician during the divided monarchy
H2139J.detail: Zaccur is a musician of the tribe of Levi, son of Asaph the famous singer. He first appears in 1 Chronicles 25:2, listed among the sons of Asaph who prophesied through music according to the orders of the king. In 1 Chronicles 25:10, he is included in the distribution of services at the temple, where his family and brothers receive their turn of duty. Many generations later, in Nehemiah 12:35, a descendant of Zaccur (Zechariah, his great-great-grandson) is seen participating with trumpets in the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem rebuilt by Nehemiah.
H2139J.origine: The name Zaccur means "he who remembers" or "memorable" in Hebrew, from the root that expresses the act of remembering. It is a theophoric name, carrying the divine meaning of memory. Zaccur's family was famous: he descended from Asaph, one of the three great musicians of temple worship under David and Solomon.
H2139J.emploi: Zaccur is mentioned three times in the provided biblical references, always in connection with his role as a Levitical musician. In 1 Chronicles 25, he is listed as the son of Asaph and a beneficiary of the distribution of service turns at the temple. In Nehemiah 12, his descendant Zechariah recalls him as an ancestor, showing that Zaccur's musical lineage continued and participated in significant moments of the restoration of Jerusalem after the exile.

sens: Jewish man at the time of the return from exile
H2139K.detail: Zabbud is an Israelite mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the Jews return from captivity in Babylon. He appears in the list of family leaders who ascend with Ezra to Jerusalem, as the son of Bigvai, accompanied by seventy men of his household (Ezra 8:14).
H2139K.origine: The name Zabbud (or Zacchur) comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to remember" or "to be attentive." It is a theophoric name, common in Israel, which reflects the idea that one should not forget God or that one entrusts God to remember. Several characters with this name appear in the Old Testament at different periods.
H2139K.emploi: Zabbud figures in the genealogy of the return from exile, one of the official lists recorded in the book of Ezra. These lists enumerate the families that leave Babylon to rebuild Jerusalem and its temple. Each family leader brings with him a contingent of his relatives and servants, which shows the importance of family as a social unit in the reconstruction of Israel after the exile.

sens: Man who helped rebuild the wall of Jerusalem after the exile
H2139L.detail: 1. Zaccur is a biblical character mentioned only once in the Bible: he is the son of Imri who participated in the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem alongside Eliashib (Nehemiah 3:2). He represents one of the many workers that Nehemiah mobilized for this great restoration project of the holy city after the return from exile in Babylon.
H2139L.origine: The name Zaccur means "remembered" or "one who is remembered," deriving its meaning from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of memory and remembrance. It is a theophoric name — that is, one that carries a religious dimension — suggesting that God remembers this character and his lineage. There are several men bearing this name in the Old Testament, but this one stands out for his concrete role in the material restoration of Jerusalem.
H2139L.emploi: Zaccur appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:2. He is listed among the workers who participated in the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem during the time of Governor Nehemiah, probably between 445 and 433 B.C. His brief but specific appearance shows that Nehemiah noted the names of the active builders, testifying to the documented and organized nature of this community restoration project.
H2139L.portee: The mention of Zaccur reminds us that the restoration of Jerusalem was not the work of a single person but of an entire community that responded to the call. His name, which means "remembered," suggests that an ordinary life of faithful service leaves a mark in God's history and in the hearts of the people.

sens: Levite who signed the covenant under Nehemiah
H2139M.detail: Zaccur is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when Nehemiah gathers the people to renew the covenant with God after the return from exile. His name appears in the list of those who sealed the covenant document (Nehemiah 10:12), indicating that he was a figure of spiritual responsibility among the Levites.
H2139M.origine: The name Zaccur means "remembered" or "memorized" in Hebrew, coming from a root that evokes the idea of keeping in memory. It is an appropriate name for a man called to remember God's covenant and to keep it alive in the hearts of the people.
H2139M.emploi: Zaccur is cited only once in the Bible (Nehemiah 10:12). He is among the Levites and leaders of the people who sealed the covenant of faithfulness to the Lord's Law after the return from exile in Jerusalem. His inscription on the document held significant value: it showed that the spiritual leaders of Israel, including the Levites, solemnly committed to walk according to God's commandments. This unique mention reveals his role as a guarantor of religious observance within the restored people.

sens: Levite during Nehemiah's time, father of Hanan
treasurer or keeper of the temple storerooms
H2139N.detail:
1. Zaccur is a Levite living during the time of Nehemiah, after the return from exile to Jerusalem. His son Hanan is named by Nehemiah among the overseers of the temple storerooms (Nehemiah 13:13).
2. Zaccur belongs to a trustworthy family of Levites: both he and his son Hanan have the reputation of being faithful and are tasked with overseeing the temple storerooms and distributing to other Levites.
H2139N.origine: The name Zaccur means "one who remembers" or "memorized" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of being kept in memory. It is a name borne by several Levites in the Bible, including a son of Asaph the musician. This sense of memory and faithfulness fits well with the Levites during Nehemiah's time, who must keep accounts of the sacred treasures.
H2139N.emploi: Zaccur appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 13:13. He is presented as the father of Hanan, a Levite whom Nehemiah chose to be the treasurer of the temple alongside Shelemiah the priest and Zadok the scribe. This mention occurs during the reform that Nehemiah undertakes to restore worship and order in the temple after the return from exile. Nehemiah's choice of Zaccur confirms the reputation for faithfulness of his family.
H2139N.portee: The figure of Zaccur and his son Hanan reminds us that God entrusts important responsibilities not by chance, but to those who have proven their faithfulness and integrity. For the Christian, this is an invitation to cultivate reliability in the tasks entrusted to them, even the simplest ones, as it is often through smallness that one gains true trust.

sens: Man whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon
Family leader of 760 exiles who returned with Zerubbabel
H2140.detail: Zaccaï is the leader of a family whose 760 descendants returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel, during the return of the people of Judah (Ezra 2:9 and Nehemiah 7:14). His name appears in the lists of exiles who returned to rebuild Jerusalem. Baruch, son of Zabbai (or Zaccaï), was one of the builders of the wall of Jerusalem after the exile (Nehemiah 3:20).
H2140.origine: The name Zaccaï means "pure" in Hebrew, derived from a root expressing purity. This name evokes purity and holiness, important qualities in post-exilic Israel.
H2140.emploi: Zaccaï is mentioned three times in the biblical texts: twice in the lists of exiles who returned (Ezra 2:9 and Nehemiah 7:14) where his family counted 760 members, and once in the person of his descendant Baruch, son of Zabbai, who participated in the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 3:20). These references place Zaccaï in the period of exile and return, around the 6th century B.C.

sens: To shine, radiate brilliance
To be clean, without stain or blemish
To be innocent, free from guilt
To be bright, clear as light
H2141.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of physical brightness: the idea of a surface that shines or radiates. Job 25:5 applies it to celestial bodies: "even the moon is not bright, and the stars are not pure in his eyes" — the word here denotes the clarity, the luminous brilliance of celestial bodies.
2. Next, the word describes material cleanliness: to be free from visible stain or dirt. Job 9:30 expresses it this way: "If I wash myself with snow, and cleanse my hands with soap" — it is the physical cleaning that makes one clean and pure.
3. The meaning expands to moral and spiritual purity: to be free from guilt or wickedness. Job 15:15 asserts that "the heavens are not pure in his sight," which means that even angels appear imperfect in God's eyes, insufficiently pure morally.
4. By extension, the word evokes clarity, transparency — a purity of brightness and truth combined: the ability to let light pass through without obstruction.
H2141.origine: The Hebrew root zakok denotes the act of shining, glowing, or sparkling. This verb is rooted in a sensory image: that of something emitting or reflecting light. The link between physical brightness and moral purity is common in the Bible: what is pure is often presented as shining, clear, and transparent. The same root has given rise to words expressing both physical and spiritual cleanliness.
H2141.emploi: The verb zakok appears only four times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the book of Job, making it a rare and particular word in ancient Hebrew wisdom. In Job 25:5, it qualifies the stars and their seemingly insufficient brightness before God. In Job 15:15, it describes the purity of celestial beings, invoked to show that no creature is truly pure before the Creator. In Job 9:30, the context is that of washing and physical cleaning, but Job uses it to express the impossibility of total purification before God. The word thus navigates between the physical reality of cleanliness and the spiritual reality of innocence, making it a key term in Job's quest for justice and divine understanding.
H2141.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that purity, in Job as in the entire Bible, is never merely a matter of external cleanliness or cleansing rituals. True purity is moral and spiritual, and it remains inaccessible to the creature in the face of God's absolute holiness. It is a lesson in humility: even our most sincere efforts at purification — washed in snow, scrubbed with soap — remain insufficient. Only God can purify; we depend on His grace and not on our own means.

sens: To keep in mind the image or memory of a person, a past event
To remind someone of a fact, a word, a promise they have forgotten or neglected
To think again of someone or something, often in a context of action or decision
To keep a written or oral account of something, to record it, to remember it
To invoke someone's name, to pronounce that name with the intention of seeking their help
H2142.detail:
1. To remember is to retain in one's memory and bring to mind something from the past. God "remembered" Noah (Genesis 8:1), which means He kept him present in His heart and acted for him. Forgetting does not exist with God; this verb expresses that someone returns to the center of His concerns and actions.
2. To remind someone is to tell or show them what they have forgotten or neglected. Moses tells the Israelites: "Remember the days of old" (Deuteronomy 32:7), so they think about what God has done for their ancestors and maintain their trust.
3. To think again is to have one's mind drawn to someone or something. When the king "thought" of Vashti (Esther 2:1), his gaze turned to her, triggering an action.
4. To record in writing or from memory is to keep a register. An "archivist" (literally "one who remembers") keeps the king's archives (Isaiah 36:3).
5. To invoke is to pronounce someone's name to summon or call for help. It is a religious act by which nations are "proclaimed" (Psalms 87:4), meaning they are mentioned before God.
H2142.origine: This verb comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of "marking," "engraving" in memory. The Hebrew word for "memorial" (zéker) belongs to the same family. To remind of something is to make it significant, like an imprint that is engraved or brought to the surface. The underlying idea is that of something that remains, that is inscribed and can be evoked.
H2142.emploi: This verb appears 223 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Torah, the Psalms, and historical narratives. It primarily denotes the act of remembering (Genesis 8:1: God remembers). It can also mean to remind others (Deuteronomy 32:7), to think of someone (Esther 2:1), or to keep a record (Isaiah 36:3). In the Psalms and Lamentations, it is a cry of the psalmist imploring God: "Lord, remember!" In particular, this verb expresses God's faithfulness to His covenant (Exodus 2:24) and the expectation that His faithful will keep His deeds in memory (Deuteronomy 8:18).
H2142.portee: For the believer, to remember is not a simple exercise of memory, but an act of trust in God. When the Bible calls to "remember" the divine wonders, it invites us to bring to mind what God has done, to strengthen faith in times of doubt. Conversely, when it says that God did not "remember" something (Lamentations 2:1), it expresses the anguish of abandonment. This verb reminds us that God acts in history and that His faithful must keep this history alive within them.

sens: What remains of someone or something in the mind and heart
The act of remembering, of not forgetting
The name, reputation, fame of a person
What perpetuates the memory, a monument or a trace
H2143.detail:
1. Memory is primarily the vivid recollection we keep of a person or an event. When Psalm 6:6 says, "the dead do not remember you anymore," it means that in death, one can no longer remember God — one has lost the ability and context to invoke Him. It is the living trace someone leaves in the hearts of the living.

2. Memory also refers to the action of remembering, the fact of keeping something present in the mind. In Deuteronomy 32:26, God says, "I will erase their memory from among men": this means wanting them to be completely forgotten, that no one recalls them to memory.

3. Memory can also be the name, reputation, what one is known and honored for. In Exodus 3:15, the Lord says, "This is my name forever, this is my name from generation to generation" — it is the enduring identity by which He will be invoked and recognized.

4. Memory is sometimes a monument, an act, or a word that perpetuates the memory of an event (Exodus 17:14 speaks of writing for "memory"), a visible mark that ensures it will not be forgotten.
H2143.origine: The Hebrew word זֵ֫כֶר comes from the root זכר ("to remember"), the same root that gives "male" (the male, one who "remembers," begets and perpetuates). Literally, memory is what keeps alive the trace of something or someone: it is the act of holding in the heart. In Greek, we encounter μνείας (mnéia, "memory") to translate this word.
H2143.emploi: This word appears 23 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms and Proverbs. Three uses emerge: first, personal memory (what one keeps of someone after their death: Psalms 34:17, 109:15); secondly, name and reputation, the way one is recognized and honored (Proverbs 10:7: "the memory of the righteous is a blessing"); finally, the mark left to avoid forgetting (Exodus 17:14, Deuteronomy 25:19). Memory can be erased by God as judgment or naturally fade after death; it can also be blessed and last forever, like that of the Lord (Psalms 135:13).
H2143.portee: This word speaks to the heart of the believer on two important points: on one hand, it reminds us that our life has weight — what we do and who we are leaves a trace, for good or for ill, in the memory of the living and before God. On the other hand, it sheds light on the vanity of pride without God: only the memory of one who clings to the Lord and His righteousness lasts forever. For the wicked, even their name is forgotten. It is a call to live in such a way as to leave a blessed memory.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the time of the united monarchy
H2144.detail: Zeker is a proper name designating a man of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is presented as the son of Abiel and Maacah, and brother of Kish, Ner, and several others. His name also appears in the form Zacharias in 1 Chronicles 9:37.
H2144.origine: The name Zeker means "memory" or "remembrance" in Hebrew, deriving from the root zkr (to remember). It is the same word that appears in the expression "for remembrance" (Exodus 13:9). The longer form of the name, Zacharias, means "the Lord has remembered." This name was common in the tribe of Benjamin.
H2144.emploi: Zeker appears only once in the biblical texts, in 1 Chronicles 8:31, in a genealogical list of the descendants of Saul. The Bible also mentions a variant of his name, Zacharias, in verse 9:37 of the same book. These genealogies are set during the time of the united monarchy of Israel.

sens: A human being or an animal of the male sex, as opposed to female
An adult man
A boy or a child of the male sex
An idol in the shape of a man (in the sense of a manufactured image)
H2145.detail:
1. The word fundamentally designates the male sex among humans and animals. In Genesis 1:27, God creates humanity "male and female," establishing this sexual distinction as part of His creation. This term also applies to animals: during the flood, Noah must bring into the ark "a male and a female of each species" (Genesis 7:9).
2. In a more restricted sense, the word designates the adult male, the man in relation to the woman. In Genesis 34:25, during the vengeance after the rape of Dinah, Simeon and Levi "killed all the males," meaning the men of the city.
3. The word can also refer to a boy or a child of the male sex. Leviticus 12:2 speaks of a woman who "bears a male." The censuses of the people (Numbers 3:15, 3:40) count "the males from one month old and above," from infants to adults.
4. Ezekiel 16:17 mentions "male idols" shaped in a context of condemnation of idolatry, where "male" refers to the masculine human form given to these statues.
H2145.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of distinction or separation, then that of what is proper to the male. The same root appears in other forms to express virility or strength. The male/female distinction is fundamental in creation according to the Bible: it appears as early as Genesis 1, as a characteristic inscribed both in human nature and in the animal kingdom.
H2145.emploi: The word appears about 80 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Torah and in the historical books. It is commonly used in the lists of the census of the people of Israel (Numbers 1, 3, 26), where males are counted from a certain age to assess the male population fit for service. It also appears in ceremonial laws: sacrifices must be "without blemish" and often "male" (Leviticus 1:3, 3:1), which specifies the quality required for the offering. The word also appears in prescriptions regarding circumcision (Genesis 17:10-14), which concerns males. In Ezra (8:3-14), the "males" returning from exile are enumerated, counting the heads of families.
H2145.portee: This word reminds us that the distinction of sex is inscribed in divine creation itself and is not an accident: God "created male and female." Through biblical usages, particularly the laws of purity and sacrifices, we also see that this sexual distinction has religious and ethical implications. Finally, the censuses show that an entire society is organized taking into account males as a structuring element of the community.

sens: That which causes one to remember something, what one keeps in memory
An object or act that recalls a person or an important event
What one leaves of oneself after death, one's trace, one's name
An act or offering intended to be presented or recalled before God
H2146.detail:
1. Remembrance is primarily what persists in memory: in Exodus 12:14, the Passover must be kept as a perpetual remembrance, meaning that future generations must always remember and celebrate it. It is to keep alive the memory of what God has done.
2. Remembrance can be a concrete object that recalls something: in Exodus 28:12, the engraved stones of the names of Israel worn on the shoulders of Aaron are a "remembrance" of the sons of Israel — they materialize before all the link of Aaron with the people.
3. Remembrance is also what remains of us, our memory, our renown after we are gone: in Ecclesiastes 1:11 and 2:16, the Preacher meditates on the fact that neither the ancients nor the wise leave a lasting remembrance — everything is forgotten.
4. Remembrance can designate a part of an offering that ascends to God to remind Him of the donor: in Numbers 5:18, the "offering of remembrance" is the portion that the priest raises to consume on the altar, as a call to God.
H2146.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to remember," "to keep in memory." It shares the same family with words like "male" (the one who is remembered, who leaves a trace) and "celebrated" (the one who is spoken of, who is memorized). The Hebrew concept of remembrance is never purely mental: it is an act of fidelity, a will not to forget what God has done, a commitment of the heart.
H2146.emploi: The word appears 22 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the legislative books (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers). It primarily designates the festivals or commemorative acts: the Passover is a perpetual remembrance (Exodus 12:14), and certain offerings include a portion of remembrance burned on the altar (Numbers 5:15, 5:18). The word also applies to objects or symbols: the names engraved on the shoulders of the high priest (Exodus 28:12), the stones from the Jordan at Gilgal (Joshua 4:7). More broadly, it designates the remembrance or renown that a person leaves after them: in Ecclesiastes, the wise man meditates on the vanity of lasting renown. Finally, it can simply mean "archives" or "annals" (Esther 6:1).
H2146.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God wants to be thanked and remembered — the festivals and acts of remembrance are not folklore, but a way to keep gratitude and faith alive. It is also an invitation to fidelity: each generation must pass on the remembrance of God's works. Finally, it humbly speaks to us of our own memory: what we leave behind is only valuable through our obedience to God, not through our own achievements.

sens: A Levite of the tribe of Levi, son of Izhar and brother of Korah
Ancestor of other Zicri mentioned in the Old Testament
H2147G.detail:
1. Zicri is a Levite who lived during the time of Egypt and the desert. He is the son of Izhar and the brother of Korah, Nepheg, and Shelomith. The Segond mentions him only once in Exodus 6:21, in the genealogical list of the descendants of Levi. His name means "memorable" or "one who is remembered."
2. The name Zicri later appears borne by several other characters in the history of Israel — some descendants of the tribe of Judah, others from Benjamin or Ephraim — who are probably his distant descendants or simply share the same family name.
H2147G.origine: The name Zicri comes from the Hebrew root that means "to remember" or "to be memorable." It is a family name, common in Levitical genealogies, which expresses the idea that the one who bears it should be memorable or worthy of remembrance.
H2147G.emploi: Zicri the Levite is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Exodus 6:21, in the genealogy of the tribe of Levi at the time of the Exodus from Egypt. He belongs to the family of Kohath, one of the three major divisions of the Levitical tribe. Later in the Old Testament, several other men bear the name Zicri — including a father of Eliezer, chief of the Reubenites during the time of David, a descendant of Judah, a descendant of Asaph the musician, and several descendants of Benjamin — but these characters live at different times and are probably not the same man.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin
Leader or warrior in ancient Israel's history
Name borne by several individuals in genealogies
H2147H.detail:
1. This name designates a man of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned in the genealogies of the people of Israel. He is the son of Shimei and has several brothers (Jakim, Zabdi, Elienai, and others), as indicated in 1 Chronicles 8:19.
2. The name "Zicri" literally means "memorable" or "one who remembers," evoking someone whose memory persists. This name was borne by several important figures at different times during the Israelite monarchy: military leaders, priests, descendants of Moses, and Levites serving in the sanctuary.
3. The biblical genealogies mention various people bearing this name, which reflects the significance of certain families in the religious and political history of Israel, particularly among the Benjaminites and the Levitical priests.
H2147H.origine: The Hebrew name זִכְרִי (Zicri) derives from the root זכר (zakhar), which means "to remember" or "to memorize." This root evokes the idea of what is enduring, of a memory that persists. Names of the same family include Zechariah (Zekhariah, "the Lord remembers") and Zacchaeus. This name emphasizes that the one who bears it is destined to be remembered, to leave a mark.
H2147H.emploi: The name Zicri appears only once in the Segond translation, in 1 Chronicles 8:19, where it designates a son of Shimei in the genealogy of Benjamin. However, the same Hebrew name is borne by several different individuals in the history of Israel: a leader of the Reubenites under David's reign, a father of Amasiah among the descendants of Judah, a son of Izhar from the line of Levites, and other figures from priestly and tribal genealogies. Each occurrence refers to a distinct period or context in biblical history, from the time of David to the reconstruction of the Temple after the exile.
H2147H.portee: This name reminds us that God remembers every human being and every lineage in His plan. The biblical genealogies, far from being mere lists, affirm that every life is inscribed in God's memory and in the history of salvation. For the believer, this means that even the most discreet names in biblical history testify to God's continuity and faithfulness to His people.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the divided monarchy
H2147I.detail: Zicri is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:23. He appears in a genealogical list of the descendants of Benjamin, listed between Abdon and Hanan as the son of Shashak. The context shows that he is a representative of this tribe at the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided between the north and the south.
H2147I.origine: The name means "memorable" or "one who is remembered," derived from the Hebrew root zâkhar (זָכַר), which means "to remember" or "to memorize." It is a theophoric name carrying the idea that a person or their deeds deserve to be remembered or remain in memory. Several biblical characters bear this name or similar variants.
H2147I.emploi: Zicri appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:23, where he is listed in the genealogy of the sons of Shashak, himself a descendant of Benjamin. This isolated mention in a genealogical list shows that Zicri was a respected ancestor of the tribe of Benjamin, worthy of being recorded in the history of God's people, even though no particular details of his life have been preserved.

sens: man of the tribe of Benjamin during the divided monarchy
H2147J.detail: Zicri is a man of the tribe of Benjamin whose name is barely mentioned in the Bible. He appears only once in the sacred text, in 1 Chronicles 8:27, where he is presented as one of the sons of Jerocham. His name means "memorable" in Hebrew, but the Bible reports nothing remarkable about him — only his genealogy is noted, as part of the register of Benjaminite families.
H2147J.origine: The name Zicri comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to remember" or "to memorize"; it expresses the idea of something or someone that deserves to be retained in memory. It is a theophoric name, meaning it is constructed to carry a religious significance, although its deeper meaning is not developed anywhere in the biblical narrative.
H2147J.emploi: Zicri appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:27, where he is listed among the descendants of Benjamin with his father Jerocham and his brothers Elijah, Jaarishiah, and others. This passage is part of a long genealogical register of the tribes of Israel, collected after the Babylonian exile. The context provides no additional information about his life, actions, or role in the history of Israel.

sens: Man of the tribe of Levi during the Exile and Return
Son of Asaph and father of Mica
Levite serving in the temple according to 1 Chronicles
H2147K.detail: 1. Zicri is a Levite mentioned for the first time in 1 Chronicles 9:15, living during the period of the Exile and the Return of Israel to Jerusalem. 2. He is the son of Asaph, a famous temple musician, and the father of Mica, placing him in an important lineage of worship servants. 3. In the biblical text, he appears as the ancestor of Matthania, who was among the Levites returned from the Return to serve in the temple of Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 9:15: "Matthania, son of Michah, son of Zicri, son of Asaph").
H2147K.origine: The name Zicri means "memorable" or "one who is remembered" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that expresses the idea of memory and remembrance. It is a typical theophoric name in Israel, reflecting the importance of the transmission of memory in the Hebrew faith. The same individual is also called Zabdi in the book of Nehemiah (11:17), a variant of the same name used in the biblical textual tradition.
H2147K.emploi: Zicri designates a high-ranking Levite in the hierarchy of temple service. He appears only once in 1 Chronicles 9:15, where he is mentioned as part of the genealogy of the Levites returned after the Exile. This genealogical mention underscores his role in the restoration of Levitical worship in Jerusalem, a crucial period for the reconstitution of the Israelite community. The text places him in the direct descent of Asaph, the chief of the temple musicians under David, indicating that he likely inherited similar liturgical responsibilities.

sens: Son of Joram, himself a descendant of Eliezer son of Moses
H2147L.detail: 1. Zicri is a Levite of the lineage of Eliezer, the son of Moses. His father is Joram and his son is Shelomith. He appears in the genealogy of the heads of Levitical families during the time of David (1 Chronicles 26:25), attesting to the importance of his family in the service of the temple.
H2147L.origine: The name Zicri means "memorable" or "one who is remembered." It comes from the Hebrew root that expresses the idea of memory and remembrance. This name reflects the importance that the people of Israel placed on remembering God and His actions.
H2147L.emploi: Zicri is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:25, where he appears in the genealogy of the Levites of the clan of Eliezer during the reign of David. His name is part of a long list of heads of temple families, indicating his role in the organization of Levitical worship.

sens: Name borne by several men in the history of Israel, notably a father of Eliezer chief of the Reubenites during the reign of King David
H2147M.detail: Zicri is a name borne by several characters in the genealogies and accounts of Israel. The most notable is Zicri, father of Eliezer who was named chief of the Reubenites under the reign of King David, as mentioned in the role of the tribe leaders in 1 Chronicles 27:16.
H2147M.origine: The name Zicri means "memorable" in Hebrew, derived from a root evoking remembrance and memory. This name reflects the importance of perpetuating the memory of ancestors and lineages in the Israelite tradition.
H2147M.emploi: Zicri appears in the genealogies of the people of Israel, particularly in the register of the tribe leaders established during David's time. The name has been borne by several descendants from different tribes, including Reubenites, Levites (descendants of Kohath), sons of Asaph, and Benjaminites. These successive appearances in genealogies show that Zicri was an honorable and recurring name among the families of Israel.

sens: man of the tribe of Judah mentioned in Chronicles
H2147N.detail: Zicri is the father of Amasiah, a military leader of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible. According to 2 Chronicles 17:16, Amasiah was the son of Zicri and commanded two hundred thousand valiant men who had willingly dedicated themselves to the service of the Lord. This passage is part of the account of King Jehoshaphat's reforms, who strengthened the army of Judah. Zicri himself plays no role in the narrated action; he is known only through his son.

sens: Prophet and priest during the time of exile and return

In Ezra 6:14, we learn that the elders of the Jews built and completed the temple according to the prophecies of Haggai and Zachariah, which shows the effectiveness of their prophetic ministry. Zachariah is mentioned only as a figure of the time of reconstruction; he should not be confused with other bearers of the same name in the Bible, notably the prophet Zachariah of the book bearing his name, who belongs to a different era.
H2148B.portee: Zachariah son of Berechiah embodies the crucial role of prophecy in times of spiritual and national crisis. His ministry, shared with Haggai, shows how God speaks through His prophets to rekindle the obedience of His people, even after exile and destruction. In the Hebrew Bible, several characters bear this name, but this one stands out as a civil leader of the return from exile.
H2148S.emploi: Zachariah appears only once in the canonical Hebrew Bible, in Ezra 8:16. He is mentioned among the leaders whom the scribe Ezra summons to form a group of officials responsible for leading the pilgrims and offerings during the return from Babylon to Jerusalem. His name appears in a list of important figures alongside other leaders like Eliezer, Ariel, and Schemaiah. This mention highlights his role as a leader in the communal restoration of the Jewish people after the exile.
H2148S.portee: This Zachariah represents believers who, after a period of separation or spiritual crisis, commit themselves to the service of return and reconstruction. His name, meaning "God remembers," reminds us that even in exile or distance, God never forsakes His people. For the Christian reader, he embodies the faithfulness to respond to God's call and to participate in the restoration of the faith community.

sens: Man who married a foreigner at the time of the return from exile
Name meaning "The Lord remembers"
H2148T.detail:
1. Zachariah is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the Israelites returned from exile and had to separate from their foreign wives. He belonged to the family of the sons of Elam and had contracted a mixed marriage (Ezra 10:26). Like many others, he had to obey the decree of separation to remain faithful to the law of Israel.

2. His Hebrew name means "The Lord remembers": a theophoric name that confesses God's memory and faithfulness to His people. It is a common name in Israel, borne by several characters in the Bible, including the prophet Zachariah and the father of John the Baptist.
H2148T.origine: The name Zachariah comes from two Hebrew words: "Zeker" (remembrance, memory) and "Yah" (abbreviation of the divine name Yahweh, the Lord). It expresses the confidence that God remembers His people and His promises. Several important figures bore this name in Israel, reflecting its pious character and popularity among Jewish families.
H2148T.emploi: This man is mentioned only in Ezra 10:26, during the return of the people from Babylon. At this critical time for the restoration of Jerusalem and the temple, religious leaders had imposed that the Israelites separate from their foreign wives to preserve the identity and religious purity of the people. Zachariah is among those who accepted this difficult measure. His sole mention shows how, even among the names of 'ordinary' people, the Bible testifies to the moral and religious challenges of the redeemed people.

sens: Man living at the time of exile and return, mentioned as an assistant to Ezra during the public reading of the Law
H2148U.detail: 1. Zachariah is a Jewish man who lived at the time of the return from exile to Jerusalem, around the 5th century B.C. He appears alongside Ezra the scribe, who read the Law of the Lord before all the assembled people. Zachariah stood to the left of Ezra on the wooden platform, among those who assisted him in this solemn reading (Nehemiah 8:4).
H2148U.origine: The name Zachariah comes from Hebrew and means "the Lord remembers" or "God remembers." It is composed of two elements: "God" and "remembers," expressing the confidence that the Lord never forgets His people or His promises.
H2148U.emploi: This man is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 8:4. He appears as one of the Levites or scribes who assisted Ezra during a major ceremony: the public reading of the Law before the people returned from captivity. This moment was crucial for the spiritual restoration of Israel after the exile. Although we know nothing else about this Zachariah, his simple name reminds us that he was a servant of God involved in reaffirming the divine covenant with His people.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah, living at the time of exile and return
Son of Amariah, father of Uzziah
H2148V.detail:
1. Zachariah is a man of Judah who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He belongs to a genealogy of notables: he is the son of Amariah and the father of Uzziah, as seen in Nehemiah 11:4, where his genealogy is listed among the first inhabitants who returned to the holy city.
2. This Zachariah, son of Amariah, is part of an important family line at the time of reconstruction. His name appears in the list of family leaders who resettled in Jerusalem, testifying to his role in the returning community.
H2148V.origine: The name Zachariah comes from Hebrew and literally means "Jehovah remembers" (from Yah, the name of God, and zachar, to remember). It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the divine name and expresses confidence in God's help. This name was borne by several important figures in the history of Israel, particularly by the prophet Zachariah, son of Berechiah and grandson of Iddo, who, along with Haggai, guided the reconstruction of the temple in the days of Zerubbabel.
H2148V.emploi: The use we have of this Zachariah is unique: he appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:4. He is cited in the genealogy of the sons of Judah who settled in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. This genealogical mention indicates that he was a family leader among the elders of Israel who returned to rebuild the nation. The context of Nehemiah places this passage during the restoration of Jerusalem under Nehemiah and Ezra, probably in the 5th century B.C.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah living after the exile to Babylon
Son of Shiloni and father of Jojarib
H2148W.detail:
1. Zachariah is a man of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the return from exile: he appears in the list of inhabitants of Jerusalem who resettled after the Babylonian captivity (Nehemiah 11:5). His name means "God remembers" in Hebrew, which expresses the confidence that God does not forget His people even in exile.
2. He is identified by his genealogy: son of Shiloni and father of Jojarib. This inscription in a lineage shows his role in the continuity of God's people at the crucial moment of return to Jerusalem.
H2148W.origine: The name Zachariah comes from Hebrew זְכַרְיָהוּ (Zekharyahou), composed of zkr ("to remember") and Yah (the divine name God). It appears frequently in the Old Testament, notably for the prophet Zachariah, son of Berechiah, who encouraged the reconstruction of the temple under Zerubbabel. This patronymic expressed hope: God remembers His covenant with Israel.
H2148W.emploi: This man named Zachariah appears only once in the provided biblical usages: in Nehemiah 11:5, in the genealogical list of families returned from exile. He is known only by this unique mention and by his place in the genealogy of Jojarib. Unlike the well-known prophet Zachariah, this Zachariah remains a secondary figure whose genealogical record alone survives.

sens: He who, at the time of the exile and return, was a priest and son of Pashhur
Man whose genealogy is recorded among the inhabitants of Jerusalem at the time of Nehemiah
H2148X.detail:
1. Zechariah is a priest living at the time of the return from exile, after the destruction of the temple in Jerusalem. His name means "The Lord remembers" — a word of hope at the very heart of exile. He is the son of Pashhur, a name known among the priestly families.
2. In Nehemiah 11:12, his name appears in the list of priests and Levites who inhabit Jerusalem again, rebuilding the temple alongside Zerubbabel. This genealogy shows how the holy families were reconstituted after the return.
H2148X.origine: The name Zechariah comes from the Hebrew זְכַרְיָהוּ (Zekaryahu), composed of זָכַר (zakar), "to remember," and יָהּ (yah), the abbreviated name of God. The name proclaims that God remembers His people — a central theme of the Exile and the Return. There is also a famous prophet of the same name, Zechariah son of Berechiah, who prophesied at the time of Zerubbabel, but this Zechariah in Nehemiah 11:12 is a different person.
H2148X.emploi: Zechariah appears only once in the provided usages, in Nehemiah 11:12, where he is named as a priest and son of Pashhur. He is part of the genealogy of Adiah, one of the leaders of the priests who returned from exile to inhabit Jerusalem and participate in the reconstruction of the temple. His inclusion in this official list emphasizes the role of the priestly families in the restoration of the Jewish community.
H2148X.portee: The name Zechariah reminds the reader that even in the midst of exile and dispersion, God does not forget His people. This simple name in a genealogical list testifies to divine faithfulness: families return, worship resumes, and the promise is fulfilled. It is a lesson in patience and trust in God's memory.

sens: Priest and prophet of the time of the return from exile
Son of Berechiah, grandson of Iddo
H2148Y.detail:
1. Zechariah is one of the twelve minor prophets of the Old Testament. He is a priest who lived after the Babylonian exile, at the time when the Israelites returned to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem. Along with the prophet Haggai, he encouraged and guided this great work of reconstruction under the authority of Zerubbabel.
2. His name means "The Lord remembers," which expresses the idea that God has not forgotten His people despite captivity. Zechariah was the son of Berechiah and the grandson of the priest Iddo (Nehemiah 12:16).
H2148Y.origine: The name Zechariah comes from the Hebrew Zekaryah, composed of two elements: "zakhar" (to remember) and "Yah" (the divine name). This composition of theophoric names (containing the name of God) was common in Israel and expressed trust in divine intervention. Several men bear this name in the Bible, but this one is best known as the prophet of the return from exile.
H2148Y.emploi: Zechariah is mentioned in Nehemiah 12:16 as a priest at the time of the return from Babylon. He is identified as the son of Berechiah and the grandson of the priest Iddo. Although the text of Nehemiah only designates him once, this Zechariah is the same person as the prophet Zechariah whose book bears his name: he prophesied and worked alongside Haggai to restore the temple, likely between 520 and 518 B.C., during the reign of the Persian king Darius.

sens: Man of the tribe of Levi, priest at the time of the return from exile
H2148Z.detail: 1. Zechariah is a priest from the family of Levi who lived at the time of Nehemiah, after the return from exile in Babylon. He is the son of Jonathan and belongs to a long lineage of priests. His name means "The Lord remembers," which expresses trust in God. The only biblical detail concerning him shows him among those who played the trumpet during the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 12:35).
H2148Z.origine: The name Zechariah comes from the Hebrew and literally means "The Lord (Yah) remembers (zachar)." It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God. It is borne by several important figures in Scripture, including the prophet Zechariah and John the Baptist according to some traditions.
H2148Z.emploi: This Zechariah is a priest mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:35, during the celebration of the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem. He is part of a brotherhood of nine children, all sons of Jonathan. His name appears in a genealogical list of the Levites who participated in the worship ceremonies at the rebuilt temple. He represents one of the many priestly families that contributed to the restoration of worship after the exile.

sens: Prophet of the time of the exile and return
Son of Berechiah and grandson of Iddo
Priest who led the reconstruction of the temple
Author of the prophetic book that bears his name
H2148v.detail:
1. Zechariah is a prophet who exercised his ministry at the time when the Jews were returning from Babylonian exile. He is first mentioned in the book of Ezra (Ezra 5:1), where he encourages the work of rebuilding the temple alongside the prophet Haggai.

2. Zechariah is the son of Berechiah and the grandson of Iddo (Zechariah 1:1). This genealogy places him in a priestly family, giving him a dual role of prophet and priest in the returning community.

3. His prophetic ministry spans several years. The words of the Lord are first addressed to him in the second year of King Darius (Zechariah 1:1 and 1:7), and again in the fourth year of the same king (Zechariah 7:1). He communicates to his people the messages and visions that God entrusts to him.

4. The book of Zechariah, the eleventh of the twelve minor prophets, contains his prophecies. His name means "The Lord remembers," which summarizes his message: God has not forgotten His people, even in exile, and fulfills His promises of restoration.
H2148v.origine: The name Zechariah comes from the Hebrew and means "Jehovah [the Lord] remembers." This name evokes God's faithfulness to His promises. In the Old Testament, several characters bear this name, but the one of interest here is Zechariah son of Berechiah, a name that is written in two slightly different forms (זְכַרְיָה and זְכַרְיָהוּ). The prophet derives his historical and spiritual importance from his mission: to proclaim that God remembers His covenant with Israel and that He brings His people back from captivity.
H2148v.emploi: Zechariah is mentioned four times in the Segond 1910, always in the book that bears his name. The first mention (Zechariah 1:1) identifies him as a prophet, son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, and situates the beginning of his ministry in the eighth month of the second year of King Darius. A second citation (Zechariah 1:7) repeats this presentation a few weeks later. The last two mentions (Zechariah 7:1 and 7:8) attest that his ministry extends to the fourth year of Darius. Zechariah fulfills his role as a prophet by receiving and transmitting the words of the Lord, notably encouraging the people to rebuild the temple and calling them to return to God.
H2148v.portee: Zechariah embodies a prophet of hope for a people weighed down by exile. His ministry alongside Haggai shows how God sends His servants to uplift His people and remind them of His promises. The meaning of his name — "The Lord remembers" — invites the believer to trust that God never forgets him, even in times of desolation or doubt.

sens: Son of the priest Jehoiada, prophet during the divided monarchy of Israel
H2148w.detail: Zechariah is a prophet and son of the priest Jehoiada, living during the time of the divided monarchy. He appears in 2 Chronicles 24:20, where he stands before the people of Judah, filled with the Spirit of God, to denounce their unfaithfulness and call them to obey the commandments of the Lord. His prophetic intervention is an act of spiritual courage in the face of a people who have forsaken God.
H2148w.origine: The name Zechariah means "the Lord remembers" or "God remembers." It combines two elements: the divine name and the idea of God's remembrance of His people. This name was borne by several biblical figures, notably the prophet of the same name among the twelve minor prophets, son of Berechiah and grandson of Iddo, who helped in the reconstruction of the temple during the time of Zerubbabel.
H2148w.emploi: Zechariah son of Jehoiada is mentioned only once in 2 Chronicles 24:20. He is a prophet of the divided monarchy, contemporary with King Joash of Judah. The Spirit of God comes upon him to deliver a word of rebuke to the people, urging them to return to the commandments of the Lord and warning them that forsaking God leads to divine abandonment.
H2148w.portee: This passage demonstrates the courage of the prophet in the face of an unfaithful people. Zechariah embodies one who, filled with the Spirit of God, dares to proclaim a difficult word to bring his people to repentance. His example reminds us that God continually calls His people to return to Him through the mouths of His prophets, even when that message is uncomfortable.

sens: Man from the tribe of Benjamin during the united monarchy
Member of the family of King Saul
H2148x.detail: 1. Zechariah is a man from the tribe of Benjamin who lived during the united monarchy (the time of the first kings of Israel). He is part of a large family whose names are listed in 1 Chronicles 9:37: he is the son of Abiel and Maacah, and has several brothers including Kish, Ner, and Gedor. This genealogy places him in the lineage of King Saul, although he himself is not a major character in history.
H2148x.origine: The name Zechariah comes from Hebrew and means "Yahweh remembers" or "the Lord memorizes." It is formed from two elements: "zeker" (memory, remembrance) and the divine name. This name expresses the confidence that God remembers His people and His promises. There are several characters bearing this name in the Bible, but this one is specifically a member of the extended family of King Saul.
H2148x.emploi: This Zechariah is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 9:37, in a genealogical list of the descendants of Saul. He is cited as one of the sons of Abiel, among his nine brothers. These genealogical lists in 1 Chronicles serve to document the influential families of Israel and to show the continuity of the people after the exile. Although we know nothing else about his personal life or deeds, his presence in this record shows his importance in the family and social structure of Israel.

sens: Prophet and priest during the time of exile and return
Rebuilder of the temple in Jerusalem with Haggai
Son of Berechiah and grandson of Iddo
H2148y.detail: 1. Zechariah is a prophet and a priest who lived during the period of the Babylonian exile and the return of the Jews to the Holy Land. His name means "Jehovah remembers," expressing the confidence that God has not forgotten His people in captivity. 2. Along with the prophet Haggai, Zechariah guided and encouraged the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem under the leadership of Zerubbabel, the Persian governor of the province of Judah, around 520 B.C. 3. He was the son of Berechiah and the grandson of the priest Iddo, indicating that he came from a family of priests and prophets. In Nehemiah 12:41, his name appears among the priests who participated in the solemn dedication of the rebuilt walls of Jerusalem, showing the esteem he held in the returning community.
H2148y.origine: The name Zechariah comes from the Hebrew Yehohanan composed of two elements: "Yah" (Jehovah, the name of God) and "zakar" (to remember). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing the piety of parents who entrust their child to divine memory. Several other men bear this name in the Old Testament, but this one is best known as the prophet who prophesied the return of the people and the reconstruction of the temple.
H2148y.emploi: The prophet Zechariah exercised his ministry around 520 B.C., in the early years of the return from exile. Along with Haggai, he encouraged Governor Zerubbabel and High Priest Joshua to rebuild the temple that the Babylonians had destroyed. His prophetic book, rich in symbolic visions, announces the future coming of the Messiah and the establishment of the kingdom of God. In Nehemiah 12:41, we see him intervening during the dedication of the walls of Jerusalem, confirming his role as a respected religious leader upon the return from exile.
H2148y.portee: Zechariah reminds believers that God always remembers His people, even in times of crisis or exile. His ministry and prophecies teach the importance of trusting in God and being zealous for the things of God, even in difficult circumstances. His example shows how faith and perseverance, with the support of other servants of God, can accomplish divine purposes.

sens: A man from the time of the divided monarchy, mentioned only once in the historical books
One whose name means "the Lord remembers"
H2148z.detail:
1. Zechariah is a man who lived during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 8:2, where the prophet Isaiah designates him as a witness to his prophetic action: "I took trustworthy witnesses, the priest Uriah, and Zechariah, son of Berechiah."

2. His Hebrew name means "the Lord remembers" or "the Lord remembers." It is a name that expresses confidence in God's faithful memory of His people.
H2148z.origine: The name Zechariah comes from two Hebrew elements: "Zakah" (to remember) and "Yah" (abbreviation of the divine name Yahweh or Lord). It is a theophoric name, meaning a name that contains the name of God. It expresses the conviction that God remembers His promises and His people. Several people have borne this name in the Bible, but Isaiah 8:2 specifically refers to a man from the 8th century B.C., father of Berechiah.
H2148z.emploi: Zechariah appears only once in the Bible: in Isaiah 8:2. The prophet cites him as a witness to his prophetic words, alongside the priest Uriah. The text tells us that he was the son of Berechiah. This unique mention, though brief, shows that he was a known and respected figure in the time of Isaiah, deemed worthy to serve as a guarantor of the prophetic word.

sens: State of that which is low, despicable, unworthy
Absence of dignity, moral nobility
Vile and ignominious conduct
H2149.detail:
1. Baseness is the state of lacking value, dignity, or esteem. It denotes what is despicable and unworthy. In its primary sense, it evokes a sort of reign or expansion of what is vile: in Psalm 12:9, it is when "baseness reigns among the sons of men" that the wicked walk freely.
2. It expresses the total absence of moral nobility in a person or in an era. It is the lowering of all that should be elevated.
3. On a concrete level, it characterizes shameful actions, low words, any behavior that degrades man far from his true dignity.
H2149.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root expressing the idea of lightness, of little value or contempt. Its starting image is that of something without weight, without importance, which opposes everything that is serious, solid, and estimable. It is the absolute opposite of nobility and honor.
H2149.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 12:9. It describes a moral state of societies: the time when baseness reigns is when the wicked prosper without restraint. The context shows that baseness is not merely a personal flaw, but an evil that "reigns" or dominates, corrupting the entirety of common life.
H2149.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize the signs of evil in the world and to refuse any form of baseness in their own thoughts, words, and deeds. When the spirit of the age encourages dishonesty or moral degradation, baseness "reigns": it is a call to remain anchored in the dignity that God confers on those who fear Him.

sens: Branch or young shoot of a vine
Flexible branch of a climbing plant
What is cut or rejected during pruning
H2150.detail:
1. The branch is a young, flexible shoot that grows on a vine. It is this green and tender part of the plant, distinct from the main trunk, that bears leaves and fruit. In Isaiah 18:5, the branch specifically refers to the limbs that the vine dresser cuts with his sickle after flowering, when the clusters begin to form and ripen.
2. More broadly, the word evokes any soft and fragile branching that extends or curls, like tendrils or stems that tremble in the wind. The image is one of natural but fleeting growth.
3. By extension, the branch symbolizes what is temporary or destined to be rejected: the limbs that are pruned and thrown away represent uselessness or divine judgment on what does not bear lasting fruit.
H2150.origine: The Hebrew word zal-zal is formed by repetition (expressive doubling) of a root that suggests the idea of trembling or vibrating — hence the primitive meaning of "that which trembles." This repetition emphasizes the effect of light vibration, of wavering flexibility characteristic of young shoots. The term belongs to the concrete vocabulary of agriculture and viticulture, central fields in biblical life.
H2150.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 18:5, in a prophetic vision concerning Ethiopia. The context is that of the growing vine: the branches are the limbs that would be pruned during the season, here rather the developing young shoots that will be cut before the harvest. The prophet uses the familiar viticultural image to describe divine judgment: just as the vine dresser removes the superfluous branches, God will remove what hinders or distracts from His true purpose.
H2150.portee: The image of the branch reminds us that external growth and visible vigor are not enough: what matters is the ripe and lasting fruit. For the believer, this word invites an evaluation of what is truly productive in their spiritual life and to accept that God prunes what seems vital but does not bear authentic fruit.

sens: To tremble, be shaken physically
To move with agitation or instability
To be troubled, destabilized internally
H2151A.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to tremble, to sway, like a mountain that shakes when God descends from heaven (Isaiah 63:19 and 64:2). It is the image of a jolt that stirs something solid, causing it to move despite its apparent solidity.
2. Figuratively, to shake means to disturb, to trouble the established order or someone's stability. When the mountains shake before God, it is because His fearsome presence disrupts every creature, even what seems unchangeable.
3. By extension, it can describe an inner disturbance, an agitation of the soul — but the biblical uses of the word focus on the physical sense and the cosmic upheaval that God's powerful coming entails.
H2151A.origine: The Hebrew verb זָלַל (zalal) evokes the idea of shaking, of making tremble. The root carries the image of unstable movement, of swaying. In the Old Testament, this verb appears mainly in contexts of majestic divine manifestation, where the earth and creatures physically react to God's presence.
H2151A.emploi: The verb is attested twice in the Segond, both in Isaiah in chapters 63-64, in the same parallel or closely related verses. In both cases, Isaiah describes the desire for God to tear open the heavens and descend: the mountains would shake before Him. It is a language of theophany, of spectacular divine manifestation that shakes all of nature. The word emphasizes how God's holy presence provokes a physical reaction in creation.
H2151A.portee: This verb reminds the reader of God's fearsome power. When even the mountains — symbols of stability and permanence — tremble before Him, it shows that nothing resists His majesty. For the Christian, it is a call to recognize God's greatness and to position oneself in humility before Him whose coming shakes the universe.

sens: Lack of restraint in the satisfaction of desires, especially wine and food
Disregard for moral values and dignity
State of degradation or humiliation
H2151B.detail:
1. Debauchery is primarily excess in the pleasures of the table and drink: one who indulges "gives in to excess and drunkenness" (Deuteronomy 21:20) or "frequents the debauchers" who waste their resources (Proverbs 23:20-21). It is unrestrained spending, the abandonment of all moderation.
2. This excess reveals a deep disregard for what has value: one who indulges in debauchery treats as vile what should be precious. The prophet Jeremiah speaks of "separating what is precious from what is vile" (Jeremiah 15:19), that is, rejecting dignity and honor.
3. Debauchery leads to degradation, to the loss of all esteem: besieged Jerusalem cries, "Look how I am humiliated" (Lamentations 1:11), for she has lost her greatness. It is the humiliation that follows self-contempt.
H2151B.origine: The Hebrew verb zahal evokes the idea of lightness, of that which weighs nothing.
