sens: To push someone or something away forcefully, to repel
To abandon someone, to cease supporting or protecting them
To no longer want someone, to disapprove of them
To set aside, to ignore
H2186A.detail:
1. To reject primarily means to physically push away or repel with determination: it is like driving someone away from oneself. In 1 Chronicles 28:9, God threatens to reject Solomon forever if he forsakes Him, an image of a definitive break.
2. The word also describes the act of abandoning someone, ceasing to support or walk with them. In Psalms 60:3, the people cry out to God: "You have rejected us, scattered us," as if the Lord left them unprotected against the enemy.
3. To reject can mean to no longer want someone, to deeply disapprove of them. In Hosea 8:3, Israel has rejected good, meaning they have despised and refused it.
4. The word is used to set aside or no longer use something. In 2 Chronicles 11:14, the Levites are rejected by Jeroboam, who removes them from their duties.
H2186A.origine: The Hebrew verb zanach comes from a root that evokes the action of throwing or pushing away. It has a definitive and violent character: it is not a simple separation, but a decided rejection. In biblical Hebrew, the word belongs to the vocabulary of rupture and judgment, often related to acts of God abandoning His people or Israel abandoning its God.
H2186A.emploi: The verb zanach appears nineteen times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated mainly in the Psalms and the prophetic books. It describes two main situations: first, God rejecting His people or one of His servants as a sign of judgment or anger (1 Chronicles 28:9, Psalms 43:2, Psalms 60:3). Secondly, the people or a person rejecting God or His commandments (Hosea 8:3). An important theme regularly recurs: the fear that God will reject His people forever, as in Psalms 77:8. But Lamentations 3:31 brings a word of hope: the Lord "does not reject forever." The word thus expresses both judgment and anxiety over the possibility of being abandoned by God.
H2186A.portee: This word reminds Christians that the relationship with God is not automatic: it requires constant faithfulness. To reject God is to refuse His commandments and His love; to be rejected by God is to suffer the consequences of sin. But Scripture also assures that God does not permanently reject His children: His rejection is never final for those who repent. It is a word of both warning and comfort.

sens: To emit a foul odor, to stink
To become repugnant, disgusting to the senses
H2186B.detail:
1. The word literally describes something that exudes a bad smell, that stinks. It is the physical image of foulness: stagnant water that corrupts and becomes fetid, like the dried-up Egyptian rivers in Isaiah 19:6, whose evaporated water leaves behind a stench and desolation.
2. By extension, it means to become odious, repugnant, detestable — not only to smell, but to endure. An infected thing provokes disgust and aversion: it is no longer just bad, it is rejected.
H2186B.origine: The Hebrew verb zanach comes from a root that evokes the release of a bad odor, decomposition. The word belongs to the semantic family of terms describing foulness and abomination. This image of the repugnant odor is linked to the broader biblical idea that moral corruption or defilement is also expressed through unpleasant sensory images.
H2186B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 19:6, in the prophecy of desolation of Egypt. It describes the Nile rivers that no longer flow, dry up, and become infected — a dramatic image of the collapse of Egyptian power and fertility. The use in the Hiphil (causative form) reinforces the idea of an action that actively produces this foulness, not accidental, but inevitable and manifest.
H2186B.portee: This word reminds us that divine desolation is not abstract: it is expressed through the concrete corruption of the world, the decay of what was once alive and fruitful. For the Christian reader, it is a warning: the absence of God's life-giving action leads to death, sterility, and repugnance. But it is also a motive of hope in the prophecies of restoration: God can bring life where corruption reigns.

sens: To jump with force and agility
To rush with vigor
To spring from one place to another
H2187.detail:
1. The verb זָנַק depicts the movement of an animal that jumps or leaps energetically — the image of a lion springing from its den to pounce on its prey. In Deuteronomy 33:22, Moses compares Dan to "a young lion that leaps from Bashan": it is the image of strength, speed, and sudden attack.
2. By extension, the word describes any vigorous thrust, any projection forward with power and determination. It is a movement that expresses vitality and dynamic power — less a slow walk than an aggressive leap.
H2187.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes jumping and leaping. The form used here (Piel) intensifies the idea: not just to jump, but to make jump, to project with force. The image is that of a wild animal — lion, gazelle — that unleashes all its muscular energy in an explosive movement. This type of action suggests freedom, raw nature, and uncontained power.
H2187.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Deuteronomy 33:22. Moses, blessing the tribes of Israel before his death, describes the tribe of Dan as a young lion that leaps from the region of Bashan. This warrior and tribal context places the word in an atmosphere of strength, vitality, and military capability. Bashan was known for its fearsome lions, making the comparison even more striking.
H2187.portee: This image of the lion leaping reminds the believer of the power and vigor that God can grant His people. The tribe of Dan is presented not as passive, but as active, capable of charging forward with strength toward its goals. It is an invitation to recognize that divine strength is not weak or hesitant, but dynamic and decisive.

sens: Liquid that flows from the skin due to heat or physical effort
H2188.detail: 1. Sweat is the liquid that beads on the skin when one is hot or working hard. The Hebrew word zeah designates this natural and visible manifestation of the body in effort or fatigue. In Genesis 3:19, God tells Adam that "by the sweat of your face you shall eat bread" — meaning that work for sustenance will be hard, costly, marked by physical exhaustion. Sweat becomes the concrete and unavoidable symbol of the effort required for life after sin.
H2188.origine: The word zeah comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of flowing or streaming. It is simple, concrete, drawn from the vocabulary of daily life: it is the body that visibly sweats when it suffers or works. This word appears only once in the Bible, precisely at the moment when God explains to humanity what its fate will now be.
H2188.emploi: The word appears only once in Genesis 3:19. It is at the decisive moment when God pronounces judgment after the sin of Adam and Eve. The sweat of the face symbolizes the exhausting effort that will be the lot of all human work on earth — not out of malice from God, but as a natural consequence of the fall: the ground will no longer yield its fruits spontaneously, and man will have to toil for sustenance. This passage establishes a biblical understanding of work: it is good in itself, ordained by God from creation, but it now bears the mark of toil.
H2188.portee: This word helps Christians accept the fatigue of daily work, not as an absurd curse, but as a just and understandable consequence of sin — and to see in effort a call to depend on God. It also gives meaning to the sweat of Jesus in Gethsemane or the agony of the Cross: the Son of God enters into this human condition of suffering and traverses it to the end to reconcile us with the Father.

sens: Intense fear, fear that seizes
State of trouble and desolation
Person or situation that provokes horror and repulsion
Spectacle of dishonor and mockery
H2189.detail:
1. Terror is a violent fear that seizes someone, a fear that paralyzes. This is what those feel who see enemy armies defeating them (Deuteronomy 28:25).
2. Terror can also refer to a state of deep trouble, of disturbance: this is what invades Judah and Jerusalem when God's anger strikes them (2 Chronicles 29:8).
3. It is also a person or a people who become an object of terror in the eyes of others — something that inspires horror and causes disgust. The unfaithful Israelites thus become a terror to all the kingdoms of the earth (Jeremiah 15:4, Jeremiah 24:9).
4. More broadly, terror encompasses dishonor, mockery, and disgrace: it is not only fear, but everything that humiliates and degrades, that others mock (Jeremiah 29:18).
H2189.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses sudden and violent movement — the shock of fear that runs through the body. It is related to words evoking trembling and agitation. The basic image is that of a person seized by a shiver of terror, and then, by extension, that of something that inspires this terror.
H2189.emploi: This word appears 7 times in the Old Testament, mostly in prophecies of calamity. It first denotes the fear that seizes a person at the moment of disaster (Deuteronomy 28:25), then the state of trouble and desolation into which God plunges His unfaithful people (2 Chronicles 29:8). But its dominant usage is this: Jeremiah and Ezekiel repeatedly use it to say that the scattered people will become an object of terror, mockery, and calamity among the nations (Jeremiah 15:4, Jeremiah 24:9, Jeremiah 29:18, Jeremiah 34:17). Thus, terror is both the reaction that the people provoke and the degrading condition in which they live.
H2189.portee: This word reminds the reader that disobedience to God has serious consequences: it transforms His people into a spectacle of horror and dishonor in the eyes of the world. It is a call to take seriously the holiness and authority of God. But for the one who returns to God, this word also shows that desolation is never final: the promise of restoration implies that one can escape this terror.

sens: Horite chief, son of Ezer and brother of Bilhan and Akan
H2190.detail: Zaavan is a Horite chief mentioned twice in the Bible, always in the genealogical lists of the ancient peoples of Canaan. He is the son of Ezer and the brother of Bilhan and Akan (Genesis 36:27; 1 Chronicles 1:42). The Horites formed a people established in Edom before the arrival of Esau, and these lists preserve the memory of their tribal leaders.
H2190.origine: The name Zaavan literally means "agitated" or "troubled." It belongs to the list of descendants of Seir the Horite, ancestors of the indigenous peoples of the mountainous region of Edom, before the Edomites (descendants of Esau) settled there.
H2190.emploi: Zaavan appears only twice in Scripture, both times in genealogical enumerations: Genesis 36:27 and 1 Chronicles 1:42. These two passages are part of the records of the Horite chiefs, that is, the princes or clan leaders who governed the region before Edomite dominance. These lists preserve a fragment of the ancient history of the peoples who inhabited Canaan before Israel.

sens: a small quantity, a small portion
a short duration, a brief moment
H2191.detail: 1. A small quantity or a small portion of something. The word denotes what is only partially or slightly present. In Job 36:2, Elihu invites his interlocutor to wait "a little" before continuing his words — he asks for a short delay that must be respected. The same image appears in Isaiah 28:10 and 28:13, where the progression of learning about God occurs "a little here, a little there": the children of Israel receive divine teaching in small successive portions, piece by piece, as one teaches a child who is just beginning to speak. 2. A short duration, a brief moment. This nuance of time appears only in Job 36:2, where "a little" means "wait a short moment"; it may refer to a simple pause before continuing.
H2191.origine: The Hebrew word זְעֵיר (zeʿir) comes from a root that means "to be or become small." It is also attested in Aramaic, a sister language of Hebrew spoken in Mesopotamia. The word denotes the small par excellence — that which lacks size, quantity, or duration. The image is one of diminishment or insufficiency.
H2191.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the Segond translation with the term "little." In Job 36:2, it qualifies a delay: Elihu asks to be listened to for a moment before he completes his discourse on the justice of God. In Isaiah 28:10 and 28:13, the prophet Isaiah uses it to describe how God teaches His people — not through great revelations all at once, but through small scattered elements, as one teaches very young children: "precept upon precept, rule upon rule, a little here, a little there." This repetition emphasizes God's progressive pedagogy with a people that refuses to listen.
H2191.portee: This word reminds us that God teaches with patience and progressiveness. He does not force those who refuse to follow Him to suddenly receive all His word, but gives it little by little — like to a child. For the Christian, it is a lesson in humility: our understanding of the mysteries of God grows slowly, in stages, and we should not expect to grasp everything at once.

sens: of small dimension or reduced importance
insignificant in appearance but proving to be powerful or threatening
H2192.detail:
1. The word denotes what is small, of reduced size. In Daniel 7:8, it is a "little horn" that arises among the other horns of the visionary beast.
2. What is small may seem unimportant at first, but can prove formidable: this little horn uproots three of the great horns and has eyes and a mouth, signs of intelligence and speech — it thus represents a hostile power that does not have the threatening appearance of its rivals but imposes itself through cunning and speech.
H2192.origine: Aramaic word (the language spoken by the Jews during the Babylonian exile) corresponding to the Hebrew זָעִיר (zair, "small"). The word belongs to the family of terms denoting smallness or youth. Daniel's vision, written in Aramaic from chapter 2 onward, uses this vocabulary to describe a spiritual reality: what appears small in human eyes can be formidable in God's sight.
H2192.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 7:8, in the vision of the four beasts and the ten horns. In this apocalyptic context, Daniel sees a "little horn" arise among the ten horns of the fourth beast. This horn, despite its initial smallness, uproots three of the first horns and has eyes and a mouth that speaks arrogantly. It symbolizes a tyrannical power that emerges unexpectedly. The use of the word "small" strongly contrasts with the power that this horn later manifests, creating dramatic tension in the vision.
H2192.portee: This passage teaches that appearances can be deceiving: what begins small and insignificant can become a major threat. For the believer, this serves as a reminder to remain vigilant against the subtle manifestations of evil or injustice, which do not always announce themselves with apparent grandeur. The prophetic vision shows that God sees and judges these powers, even if they seem emerging or hidden from human eyes.

sens: To gradually extinguish, to disappear like a flame that goes out
To cease, to come to an end
To lose strength, intensity, to weaken
H2193.detail:
1. The word paints the image of a flame that gradually goes out: it is a progressive and inevitable disappearance. In Job 17:1, Job speaks of his days that are extinguishing like a light that is fading — the image evokes the imminent end, the decline towards death.
2. The meaning broadens to encompass any cessation, any stopping: something that was burning, that was alive, that was active stops and disappears.
3. The disappearance can be that of vital force, energy, or hope that slowly diminishes before completely ceasing.
H2193.origine: The Hebrew word יָאַךְ comes from a root expressing gradual extinction. It evokes the natural and ancient image: that of fire which, without fuel, diminishes and disappears. It is a descriptive root of observable reality, one of the fundamental images of death and decline in the Bible.
H2193.emploi: The word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Job 17:1. Job uses it in his discourse of extreme suffering: his days are extinguishing like a lamp, his breath is lost. It is a verb in the passive voice (it undergoes extinction) that expresses not a violent action but an inexorable weakening. The context of Job suits this choice: it is not a sudden death, but a slow agony.
H2193.portee: This word challenges the reader about the fragility of human life. It reminds us that our existence is fragile, limited, destined to extinguish — a truth that the Bible never hides. It invites us to seek the meaning that lasts, beyond this earthly light that goes out. For the Christian, it contrasts with the promise of eternal life in Christ.

sens: To feel indignation, to be angry, irritated or furious
To express one's indignation, anger in words; to curse, to condemn
To provoke indignation, irritation in someone
H2194.detail:
1. The most common meaning is that of a sharp irritation, a anger that seizes someone: God himself "is irritated" when justice is trampled (Psalms 7:12). It is a feeling of indignation in the face of what is wrong or offensive.
2. The word also designates the expression of this anger through strong words: to curse, to publicly condemn. Balaam is urged to curse Israel, but he refuses to express indignation against a people that God blesses (Numbers 23:7-8). To denounce someone is to express one's irritation against them through words.
3. Finally, the word can describe what provokes indignation: an irritated face (Proverbs 25:23) or being oneself the object of God's or others' anger and curse (Proverbs 22:14, Proverbs 24:24).
H2194.origine: The Hebrew root designates moral indignation, the energetic protest of a person in the face of injustice or offense. The word evokes the image of anger that expresses itself, that comes out of oneself to strike another or one's honor. The family of the word includes the noun זַעַם (indignation, anger, curse), which emphasizes the passionate and moral character of this reaction.
H2194.emploi: This verb appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Proverbs and wisdom literature, but also in the prophets. It describes sometimes the indignation one feels (Psalms 7:12: God is irritated at all times), sometimes that which one expresses against others (Numbers 23:7-8: to curse), sometimes that which one suffers (Proverbs 22:14, 24:24: to be cursed, condemned). Generally, the subject is a person of power — God, a king, a wise people — who manifests moral indignation.
H2194.portee: This word reminds us that indignation is not always sin: God himself is irritated in the face of injustice and rebellion. It is the echo of divine justice. But for the believer, it is also a warning: one who tramples justice risks provoking indignation, the curse of the righteous judge. It is an invitation not to make oneself detestable through evil.

sens: Violent emotion, burning wrath and indignation
Divine fury manifested in judgment
Intention to reject, to push away violently
Punishment or destruction sent as an expression of anger
H2195.detail:
1. The word zaàm primarily designates anger as a vivid and passionate emotion: an indignation that boils. In Psalms 38:4, the psalmist asks God to withdraw his anger, for it even affects his body. It is a anger that acts, that devastates.

2. Very often, zaàm describes the anger of God — not an impulsive reaction, but the indignation of his justice in the face of evil. In Isaiah 13:5, God and his instruments of anger march to destroy the land; in Jeremiah 10:10, the earth trembles before the anger of the Lord.

3. The word can also express violent rejection, abandonment: in Lamentations 2:6, God in his violent anger has rejected the king and the priest, that is to say, he has removed them, stripped them of their functions.

4. By extension, zaàm designates the punishment or destruction itself, the concrete effect of divine anger. In Ezekiel 22:31, God pours out his fury and consumes by the fire of his anger.
H2195.origine: The word zaàm comes from a root that expresses the idea of growling, manifesting violent indignation. It is linked to the image of wrath that boils and comes out of oneself. The root also evokes the action of pushing away, rejecting: one drives away from oneself that which provokes this indignation. Zaàm appears throughout Scripture to speak of anger, especially that of God towards sin.
H2195.emploi: Zaàm appears 22 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. It is a word that primarily describes divine anger. In Psalms 38:4 and 102:11, the believer cries under the weight of God's anger directed against him because of his sin. In the prophets — Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Nahum — zaàm becomes an active force: God deploys his anger as a weapon against rebellious nations (Isaiah 13:5), and it consumes, destroys, repels. In Lamentations 2:6, the meaning shifts towards rejection: anger manifests itself by abandoning its people. The word can also designate the punishment itself, the visible effect of this divine indignation.
H2195.portee: For the biblical reader, zaàm reminds us that the anger of God is not a capricious passion, but the expression of his justice in the face of evil and sin. It is a formidable reality, from which one cannot escape unpunished. But the Bible does not stop at anger: it also announces forgiveness and grace. Recognizing the reality of divine anger helps the believer take sin seriously and seek reconciliation.

sens: To become angry, to be furious
To be upset, dissatisfied, in a bad mood
To appear sad, downcast, discouraged
H2196.detail:
1. To become irritated means to enter into a fierce anger, a sudden rage. The Bible clearly shows this when anger seizes King Uzziah: he becomes irritated against the priests who oppose him, so much so that his rage triggers divine punishment (2 Chronicles 26:19). It is a violent and visible feeling.

2. The word also describes the state of someone who is upset, dissatisfied, who is brooding. The foolish man becomes irritated against the Lord when his folly distorts his way (Proverbs 19:3): he is in inner revolt. It is less about explosive fury than about a dark and bitter mood.

3. To become irritated can mean to appear sad or downcast, the expression on the face changes. When Joseph observes the two officers of Pharaoh, he sees that they are sad (Genesis 40:6), the word making this change visible. Daniel fears that his face will be more downcast than that of the other young men because of the imposed diet (Daniel 1:10): the outward appearance reflects the inner state.
H2196.origine: The Hebrew verb זָעַף (zaph) comes from a root evoking the idea of trouble, emotional disturbance. It paints a rupture in inner balance: whether violent (anger) or silent (sadness), it shows on the face and in behavior. The root is attested in strong emotional contexts, always linked to a disruption of well-being or mood.
H2196.emploi: The verb zaph appears four times in the Hebrew Bible. It describes very concrete emotional states: the furious anger of King Uzziah who becomes irritated against the priests (2 Chronicles 26:19), the inner revolt of the foolish man who becomes irritated against God (Proverbs 19:3), the sad faces of Pharaoh's officers (Genesis 40:6), and the downcast appearance that Daniel fears (Daniel 1:10). The word navigates between two poles: explosive anger on one side, melancholy and discouragement on the other, but always with a visible expression, a disturbance of the normal state.
H2196.portee: This verb shows us that anger and sadness are never buried: they are read on the face and influence our behavior. For the believer, this reminds us that irritation against God or the circumstances of life is a sin that manifests itself. It is also a call to examine our expressions and attitudes: what do they reflect about our heart state and our trust in God?

sens: Fit of rage, explosion of violent fury
Persistent wrath, lasting indignation
Combative fervor, destructive impulse in action
Storm, violent agitation of nature
H2197.detail:
1. It is primarily a sudden explosion: King Asa becomes furious against the seer and throws him in prison (2 Chronicles 16:10), seized by a rage that causes him to lose control. Anger here is a violent and immediate outburst.
2. But it is also an indignation that lasts and persists: Micah accepts to bear "the anger of the Lord" (Micah 7:9) as a just punishment that must be endured until God judges him. It is a firm, heavy anger that extends over time.
3. Anger can be a devastating fervor: the Lord makes His voice heard "in the fervor of His anger" (Isaiah 30:30), with flames, hail, and the storm. It is a force that unfolds, strikes, and destroys.
4. The word also designates the violent agitation itself: the "fury of the sea" calms when Jonah is thrown into the water (Jonah 1:15), the sea rages and calms like a living being in anger.
H2197.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses boiling, heating, agitation. It is the image of water boiling or a being coming to a boil. The word is related to other Hebrew terms designating fury and indignation, and it literally translates the idea of a rising heat, a tension that explodes.
H2197.emploi: This word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Chronicles, the Prophets, and Wisdom literature. It describes the anger of kings (Asa, the king in general), that of the Lord against His people, and even the fury of nature. In 2 Chronicles 28:9, the anger of God is presented as the cause of a military defeat: God delivers Judah into the hands of its enemies. In Proverbs 19:12, royal anger is compared to the roaring of a lion, highlighting its fearsome character. In Isaiah 30:30, it is a cosmic anger accompanied by terrifying phenomena. The word thus designates both a human emotion and a divine reality.
H2197.portee: The word shows that anger, although it can be just (that of God in the face of sin), is also a danger: it drives Asa to imprison a prophet, it destroys peoples. For the Christian reader, it reminds us that the anger of God is real, that it has serious consequences, but also that it can be borne if one turns to His justice (Micah 7:9). This invites repentance rather than rebellion.

sens: State of strong displeasure, bad mood
Suppressed anger, contained within oneself
H2198.detail: 1. The word describes someone who is upset, dissatisfied, in a bad mood — not an explosive anger, but an irritation that manifests itself through withdrawal and bitterness. In 1 Kings 20:43, the king of Israel leaves the battlefield sad and irritated because he did not get what he wanted. 2. It is a contained anger that takes hold of the heart and colors all behavior. In 1 Kings 21:4, Ahab, irritated that he cannot possess Naboth's vineyard, lies down, turns his face away, and refuses to eat: his irritation affects his whole body, it paralyzes him.
H2198.origine: The Hebrew word zaèph comes from a root that expresses the idea of frowning, wrinkling (the forehead, the face) — as one does involuntarily under the effect of displeasure. This image of a face tightened by dissatisfaction is at the heart of the word: one recognizes someone who is irritated by their closed and tense expression.
H2198.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both times in 1 Kings and concerning kings: Ahab is the princely example. In both cases, the irritation arises from frustration — not achieving victory, not being able to conquer land — and it leads to a sulking attitude. It is not an explosion of rage, but a prolonged dark mood.
H2198.portee: This word teaches us that the heart of the believer can become corrupted by small irritations that do not resolve. Ahab, irritated, becomes blind to reality; he harms himself by closing off. The Word of God invites us not to let irritation take root, but to entrust it to God rather than to brood over it.

sens: To let out a cry, a loud exclamation
To call for help, to implore
To complain, to groan under suffering
To summon, to gather by a call
To proclaim, to announce aloud
H2199.detail:
1. To let out a cry or a loud exclamation: this is the physical act of emitting a loud sound with the voice, as the children of Israel "cried out" under the Egyptian yoke (Exodus 2:23), or as the cities "cry out" during a calamity (Isaiah 15:4).
2. To call for help, to implore someone: the cry becomes a supplication addressed to God or to a man, like the Israelites who cry out to God in times of distress (Judges 6:7) or the faithful who cry out to God in the Psalms (Psalms 107:13).
3. To complain, to groan, to express pain: the cry is the raw expression of suffering, like that of a woman in labor who "cries out" (Isaiah 26:17).
4. To summon, to gather by a call: the cry becomes a signal, an order: Saul gathers the people (1 Samuel 14:20), or Joel calls to summon an assembly (Joel 1:14).
5. To proclaim, to announce publicly: the cry becomes a message: "Let out groans and cries! Publish on the Arnon" (Jeremiah 48:20).
H2199.origine: The Hebrew root צעק (zaaq) likely imitated the sound of the cry itself. The word appears in the closely related Aramaic (ze.iq) with the same meaning. In Hebrew, the same family of words is found to express urgency and direct calling: it is a visceral verb that expresses what cannot be held back.
H2199.emploi: The verb zaaq is one of the most common words in the Old Testament to express the cry or call (73 occurrences). It mainly occurs in three contexts: first, physical or moral distress, when Israel cries under oppression (Exodus 2:23) or when the faithful cry out to God in the Psalms; second, military or civil calling, when gathering the people (1 Samuel 14:20, Joel 1:14); finally, proclamation, especially among the prophets who announce the words of God. The word does not change its fundamental meaning, but the context determines whether it is a personal supplication, an order, or a public proclamation.
H2199.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible acknowledges the cry as a legitimate human reaction to suffering and injustice. It also shows that the cry that rises to God is never unanswered: God hears, God comes. For the Christian today, it is an invitation to cry out to God without shame, in distress as well as in joy, knowing that God listens to the cry of those who call upon Him.
